Can it be true?” “Dear Uncle,” said K., wrenching himself out of his distraction, “I don't even know what you want from me.” “Josef,” his uncle said warningly, “you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Am I to take your last words as a bad sign?” “I can guess what you want,” K. said obediently. “You've probably heard about my case.” “That's right,” his uncle replied, nodding slowly. “I've heard about your case.” “From whom?” K. asked. “Erna wrote to me about it,” said his uncle. “She has no contact with you—you don't take much interest in her, unfortunately—but she found out all the same. I got the letter today and of course came straight here. For no other reason, but it seems reason enough. I can read you the passage about you.” He took the letter from his wallet. “Here it is. She writes: ‘I haven't seen Josef for a long time. Last week I went to the bank once, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't admitted. I waited nearly an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak to him; perhaps there'll be an opportunity soon. He sent me a large box of chocolates for my name day. It was very kind and thoughtful. I forgot to write and tell you at the time; only now that you ask do I remember. You must understand that chocolates disappear immediately at the boarding school. Scarcely have you realised that someone has given you chocolates when they're already gone. But about Josef, there was something else I wanted to tell you. As I mentioned, they wouldn't let me see him at the bank because he was in discussion with a gentleman. After waiting quietly for a while, I asked an attendant whether the discussion would last much longer. He said it probably would, because it was most likely about the case being brought against the authorised signatory. I asked what sort of case it was and whether he was mistaken, but he said he was not mistaken; it was a case, and a serious one, though he knew nothing more. He would gladly help the authorised signatory himself, since he was a good and fair gentleman, but he didn't know how to set about it and could only hope that influential gentlemen would take him under their protection. That was sure to happen, and everything would turn out well in the end, but for the present, judging by the authorised signatory's mood, things weren't going at all well. Naturally I attached little importance to this talk, tried to reassure the simple-minded attendant, forbade him to speak of it to others, and consider the whole thing gossip. Still, perhaps it would be good, dearest Father, if you looked into the matter on your next visit. It would be easy for you to find out more precisely what is happening and, if it really should be necessary, intervene through your important and influential acquaintances. But if it isn't necessary, which is the most likely thing, at least it will soon give your daughter a chance to embrace you, which would make her happy.’” “A good child,” said his uncle when he had finished reading, wiping a few tears from his eyes. K. nodded. With all the disturbances of recent weeks he had completely forgotten Erna, even her birthday, and the story of the chocolates was plainly invented to protect him before his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and certainly not sufficiently repaid by the theatre tickets he intended to send her regularly from now on, but he did not feel suited at present to visits at the boarding school and conversations with a little eighteen-year-old schoolgirl. “And what do you say now?” asked his uncle, who had forgotten all his haste and agitation over the letter and seemed to be reading it again. “Yes, Uncle,” said K., “it's true.” “True?” his uncle cried. “What's true? How can it be true? What sort of case? Surely not a criminal case?” “A criminal case,” K. replied. “And you're sitting here calmly with a criminal case hanging over your head?” his uncle cried, growing louder and louder. “The calmer I am, the better for the outcome,” K. said tiredly. “Don't be afraid.” “That doesn't reassure me,” his uncle exclaimed. “Josef, dear Josef, think of yourself, of your relatives, of our good name. Until now you've been our pride; you mustn't become our shame. Your attitude”—he looked at K. with his head tilted sideways—“doesn't please me. This isn't how an innocent accused man behaves while he still has his strength. Just tell me quickly what it's about, so I can help you. It concerns the bank, of course?” “No,” said K., standing up. “But you're speaking too loudly, dear Uncle. The attendant is probably at the door listening. I find that unpleasant. We'd better go out. Then I'll answer all your questions as well as I can. I know very well that I owe the family an account.” “Right!” his uncle shouted. “Quite right. Only hurry, Josef, hurry.” “I just have to give a few instructions,” said K., summoning his deputy by telephone. He came in within moments. In his agitation the uncle gestured to show him that K. had sent for him, though there could have been no doubt about that anyway. Standing in front of his desk, K. quietly explained to the young man, who listened coolly but attentively, what still had to be done that day in his absence, referring to various documents. His uncle was a disturbance, first standing beside them with wide eyes, nervously biting his lips, without actually listening, though the appearance of listening was disturbing enough. Then he walked about the room, stopping now and then before the window or a picture, continually breaking into exclamations such as “I find it completely incomprehensible,” or “Just tell me now, what's to become of it?” The young man acted as though he noticed none of this, calmly listened to all K.'s instructions, made a few notes, and left after bowing to both K. and his uncle, who at that moment had his back turned, was looking out of the window and was crumpling the curtains in his outstretched hands. The door had scarcely closed when his uncle exclaimed: “At last that puppet's gone. Now we can go too. At last!” Unfortunately there was no way of persuading him to stop asking about the case in the entrance hall, where several employees and attendants stood about and which the deputy manager was just crossing. “Now, Josef,” his uncle began, returning the bystanders' bows with slight salutes, “tell me openly what sort of case it is.” K. made a few meaningless remarks and even laughed a little; only on the stairs did he explain to his uncle that he had not wanted to speak openly in front of people. “Right,” said his uncle. “But speak now.” With his head bent, smoking a cigar in short, hurried puffs, he listened. “First of all, Uncle,” said K., “this isn't a case before an ordinary court at all.” “That's bad,” said his uncle. “What?” said K., looking at him. “I mean that's bad,” his uncle repeated. They were standing on the outside steps leading to the street. Since the porter seemed to be listening, K. drew his uncle down, and the busy street traffic took them in. His uncle, who had linked arms with K., no longer pressed so urgently about the case; they even walked on in silence for a while. “But how did it happen?” he finally asked, stopping so suddenly that the people behind him dodged aside in alarm. “Things like this don't happen suddenly. They build up over a long time. There must have been signs. Why didn't you write to me? You know I'll do anything for you. In a way I'm still your guardian, and until today I was proud of it. Of course I'll still help you now, but now that the case is already under way, it's very difficult. In any event, the best thing would be for you to take a little leave and come to us in the country. You've grown a little thin too; I notice it now. You'll regain your strength in the country, and that will be good, since there are certainly exertions ahead of you. Besides, you'll be removed from the court's reach to some extent. Here they have every sort of means of exerting power, which they necessarily and automatically apply to you as well; but to reach the country they would first have to send representatives, or merely try to influence you by letter, telegram or telephone. Naturally that weakens the effect. It doesn't free you, but it lets you breathe.” “They could forbid me to leave,” said K., drawn somewhat into his uncle's line of thought by his speech. “I don't think they'll do that,” his uncle said thoughtfully. “The loss of power they suffer through your departure wouldn't be so great.” “I thought,” said K., taking his uncle under the arm to stop him from standing still, “you would attach even less importance to the whole thing than I do, and now you're taking it so seriously yourself.” “Josef!” his uncle cried, trying to free himself so that he could stop, but K. would not let him. “You've changed. You always had such sound understanding, and now, of all times, it deserts you? Do you want to lose the case? Do you know what that means? It means you're simply struck out. And the whole family is dragged down with you, or at least humiliated to the ground. Josef, pull yourself together. Your indifference is driving me out of my mind. Looking at you, one could almost believe the saying: ‘To have a case like that is already to have lost it.’” “Dear Uncle,” said K., “agitation is so useless, on your part and as it would be on mine. Cases aren't won by agitation. Give my practical experience a little credit, as I always respect yours, even when it surprises me, and do now as well. Since you say the family too would be affected by the case—which I for my part can't understand at all, but that's secondary—I'm happy to follow your advice in everything. Only I don't consider a stay in the country advantageous, even from your point of view, since it would signify flight and a sense of guilt. Besides, although I'm pursued more here, I can also do more about the matter myself.” “Right,” said his uncle, in a tone suggesting they were at last drawing closer. “I only made the suggestion because, if you stayed here, I saw the matter endangered by your indifference and thought it better for me to work on your behalf in your place. But if you intend to pursue it yourself with all your strength, that's naturally much better.” “Then we're agreed on that,” said K. “And do you have a suggestion now as to what I should do first?” “Naturally I still have to think it over,” said his uncle. “You must remember that I've lived almost continuously in the country for twenty years now, and that makes one's instincts in these directions grow dull. Various important connections with people who might understand things better here have loosened of their own accord. I'm a little isolated in the country, as you know. One only really notices it on occasions like this. Your affair also came partly as a surprise to me, although, strangely enough, after Erna's letter I already suspected something of the kind, and today at the sight of you I knew it almost for certain. But that doesn't matter. The most important thing now is not to lose time.” Even while speaking he had stood on tiptoe and waved to a car, and now, calling an address to the driver, he pulled K. in after him. “We're going to the lawyer Huld,” he said. “He was a schoolmate of mine. You must know the name too? No? That's strange. He has a considerable reputation as a defence lawyer and a lawyer for the poor. But I have particular confidence in him as a person.” “Whatever you do is all right with me,” said K., though his uncle's urgent haste in dealing with the affair made him uneasy. There was nothing particularly pleasant about going as an accused man to a lawyer for the poor. “I didn't know,” he said, “that one could engage a lawyer in a matter like this.” “Of course,” said his uncle. “It goes without saying. Why not? And now tell me everything that's happened so far, so I'm fully informed.” K. immediately began his account, concealing nothing. His complete frankness was the only protest he could allow himself against his uncle's view that the case was a great disgrace. He mentioned Miss Bürstner's name only once, briefly, but that did not impair his frankness, for Miss Bürstner had no connection with the case. As he spoke, he looked out of the window and noticed that they were approaching the very suburb where the court offices were. He pointed this out to his uncle, who did not find the coincidence particularly striking. The car stopped before a dark house. His uncle immediately rang at the first door on the ground floor. While they waited, he bared his large teeth in a smile and whispered: “Eight o'clock—an unusual time for a client's visit. But Huld won't hold it against me.” Two large black eyes appeared at the peephole, examined the two visitors for a little while, and vanished, but the door did not open. The uncle and K. confirmed to each other that they had seen the eyes. “A new maid who's afraid of strangers,” said his uncle, knocking again. The eyes reappeared; now one could almost have thought them sad, though perhaps that was only a deception caused by the open gas flame burning just above their heads with a loud hiss but little light. “Open up!” his uncle shouted, pounding the door with his fist. “We're friends of the lawyer.” “The lawyer is ill,” came a whisper behind them. A gentleman in a dressing gown stood in a doorway at the other end of the little passage, delivering this information in an extremely quiet voice. The uncle, already furious at the long wait, spun round and exclaimed: “Ill? You say he's ill?” advancing almost threateningly towards the gentleman, as though he were the illness. “They've opened the door,” said the gentleman, pointing towards the lawyer's door, gathering his dressing gown around him and disappearing. The door had indeed been opened. A young girl—K. recognised the dark, slightly protruding eyes—stood in the entrance hall wearing a long white apron and holding a candle. “Next time, open sooner,” said his uncle instead of greeting her, while the girl made a little curtsey. “Come, Josef,” he then said to K., who slowly edged past her. “The lawyer is ill,” the girl said, as his uncle hurried without stopping towards a door. K. was still staring at her even as she turned to lock the apartment door again. Her face was rounded like a doll's; not only her pale cheeks and chin were round, but her temples and the edges of her forehead too. “Josef,” his uncle called again, then asked the girl: “Is it his heart condition?” “I believe so,” she said. She had found time to go ahead with the candle and open the room's door. In a corner the candlelight had not yet reached, a face with a long beard rose from a bed. “Leni, who's coming?” asked the lawyer, who, dazzled by the candle, did not recognise his guests. “It's Albert, your old friend,” said the uncle. “Oh, Albert,” said the lawyer, sinking back onto his pillows as though this visitor required no pretence. “Is it really so bad?” asked the uncle, sitting on the edge of the bed. “I don't think so. It's an attack of your heart trouble, and it'll pass like the earlier ones.” “Possibly,” the lawyer said quietly. “But it's worse than ever before. I find it hard to breathe, I don't sleep at all, and I lose strength every day.” “I see,” said the uncle, pressing his Panama hat firmly against his knee with his large hand. “That's bad news. Are you being properly cared for, though? It's so sad here, too, so dark. It's a long time since I was last here; it seemed more cheerful then. Your little young lady here doesn't seem very cheerful either, unless she's pretending.” The girl still stood near the door with the candle. So far as her indeterminate gaze allowed one to tell, she was looking more at K. than at his uncle, even when he spoke about her. K. leaned against a chair he had pushed near her. “When one is as ill as I am,” said the lawyer, “one needs quiet. It doesn't seem sad to me.” After a short pause he added: “And Leni looks after me well. She's a good girl.” But that did not convince the uncle. He was visibly prejudiced against the nurse, and though he did not contradict the sick man, he followed her with stern eyes as she went to the bed, set the candle on the bedside table, leaned over the patient and whispered to him while arranging his pillows. Almost forgetting consideration for the sick man, he rose and paced behind the nurse. K. would not have been surprised if he had caught her skirts from behind and pulled her away from the bed. K. himself watched everything calmly. The lawyer's illness was not even entirely unwelcome to him. He had been unable to oppose the zeal his uncle had developed for his case, and gladly accepted the diversion that zeal now found without any effort on his part. Then his uncle said, perhaps solely to insult the nurse: “Miss, please leave us alone for a little while. I have a personal matter to discuss with my friend.” The nurse, still bent far over the patient and at that moment smoothing the sheet by the wall, merely turned her head and said very calmly, in striking contrast to the uncle's words, which faltered with rage and then poured out again: “You can see the gentleman is so ill; he can't discuss matters.” She had probably repeated his words only for convenience, but even an uninvolved observer could have taken it as mockery, and naturally the uncle jumped as though stung. “You damned woman,” he said, still rather indistinctly in the first gurgle of agitation. K. was startled, though he had expected something of the kind, and hurried towards his uncle with the firm intention of closing his mouth with both hands. Fortunately, however, the patient rose behind the girl. The uncle's face darkened as though he were swallowing something revolting, and he then said more calmly: “Naturally we haven't lost our reason either. If what I ask were impossible, I wouldn't ask it. Please go now.” The nurse stood upright beside the bed, fully facing the uncle; with one hand, as K. thought he noticed, she stroked the lawyer's hand. “You can say anything in front of Leni,” said the patient, unmistakably in the tone of an urgent plea. “It doesn't concern me,” said the uncle. “It's not my secret.” He turned away as though intending to negotiate no further, but allowing a little time for thought. “Whom does it concern, then?” asked the lawyer in a fading voice, lying back again. “My nephew,” said the uncle. “I've brought him along.” And he introduced him: Josef K., authorised signatory. “Oh,” said the patient much more briskly, holding out his hand to K., “forgive me, I hadn't noticed you at all. Go, Leni,” he then said to the nurse, who no longer resisted, offering her his hand as though they were parting for a long time. “So,” he finally said to the uncle, who had come closer, reconciled, “you haven't come to visit a sick man; you've come on business.” It was as though the idea of a sick visit had paralysed the lawyer until now, so much stronger did he look. He remained constantly propped on one elbow, which must have been fairly strenuous, and kept tugging a strand in the middle of his beard. “You already look much healthier,” said the uncle, “now that witch is outside.” He broke off, whispered, “I'll bet she's listening,” and sprang to the door. But no one was behind it. The uncle returned, not disappointed, since her failure to listen struck him as still greater malice, but embittered. “You misjudge her,” said the lawyer, without defending the nurse further; perhaps he meant to suggest she needed no defence. But he continued in a far more concerned tone: “As for your nephew's affair, I would certainly count myself fortunate if my strength proved equal to this exceptionally difficult task. I very much fear it won't. In any event, I shall leave nothing untried; if I'm not equal to it, someone else could be brought in as well. To be frank, the affair interests me too much for me to bring myself to forgo all involvement. If my heart can't bear it, at least it will find here a worthy occasion to fail completely.” K. felt he understood not a word of this speech. He looked at his uncle for some explanation, but the uncle sat holding the candle on the bedside table, from which a medicine bottle had already rolled onto the carpet, nodding at everything the lawyer said, agreeing with it all, and looking now and then at K. with an invitation to agree too. Had his uncle perhaps told the lawyer about the case before? But that was impossible; everything that had happened spoke against it. “I don't understand—” he therefore said. “Have I perhaps misunderstood you?” asked the lawyer, as surprised and embarrassed as K. “Perhaps I was too hasty. What did you want to discuss with me? I thought it concerned your case?” “Of course,” said his uncle, then asked K.: “What do you want?” “Yes, but how do you know anything about me and my case?” K. asked. “Oh, I see,” the lawyer said with a smile. “I am a lawyer, after all; I move in court circles. Various cases are discussed, and the more striking ones stay in one's memory, particularly when they concern a friend's nephew. There's nothing strange about that.” “What do you want?” his uncle asked K. again. “You're so restless.” “You move in those court circles?” K. asked. “Yes,” said the lawyer. “You ask questions like a child,” said his uncle. “Whom should I associate with, if not people in my own profession?” the lawyer added. It sounded so irrefutable that K. made no reply. He had wanted to say: “But you work at the court in the Palace of Justice, not the one in the attic,” yet could not bring himself actually to say it. “You must remember,” the lawyer continued, in a tone as though he were explaining something obvious, unnecessarily and in passing, “you must remember that I also draw great advantages for my clients from such associations, in many respects, and one can't even always speak of them. Naturally my illness hampers me a little just now, but good friends from the court still visit me and I hear a few things. Perhaps I hear more than some people in the best of health who spend all day at court. For example, I have a dear visitor at this very moment.” He pointed to a dark corner of the room. “Where?” K. asked, almost rudely in his initial surprise. He looked around uncertainly; the little candle's light came nowhere near the opposite wall. And indeed something began to stir in that corner. In the light of the candle, which the uncle now held high, an elderly gentleman could be seen sitting at a little table. He could hardly have breathed, to have remained unnoticed so long. Now he rose laboriously, evidently displeased at having attention drawn to him. It was as though, with his hands moving like short wings, he wanted to fend off all introductions and greetings, as though he wished on no account to disturb the others by his presence, and urgently begged to be returned to the darkness and forgotten again. But that could no longer be granted. “You surprised us, you see,” the lawyer explained, encouragingly beckoning the gentleman closer, which he did slowly, hesitantly, looking about, yet with a certain dignity. “The chief clerk—oh, forgive me, I haven't introduced you—this is my friend Albert K., this his nephew Josef K., authorised signatory, and this the chief clerk—the chief clerk was kind enough to visit me. Only someone on the inside, who knows how overwhelmed with work our dear chief clerk is, can really appreciate the value of such a visit. Well, he came nevertheless. We were talking peacefully, as far as my weakness allowed. We hadn't actually forbidden Leni to admit visitors, since none were expected, but we had intended to remain alone. Then came your pounding fists, Albert. The chief clerk moved with his chair and table into the corner. But now it turns out that we may, that is if there is a wish to do so, have business in common to discuss and can very well draw together again.—Chief Clerk,” he said, bowing his head with a submissive smile and indicating an armchair near the bed. “Unfortunately I can stay only a few minutes longer,” said the chief clerk pleasantly, settling expansively into the armchair and looking at his watch. “Business calls. In any case, I don't want to let the opportunity pass to meet a friend of my friend.” He inclined his head slightly towards the uncle, who seemed very pleased with the new acquaintance but, by his nature unable to express feelings of deference, accompanied the chief clerk's words with embarrassed but loud laughter. An ugly sight! K. could observe everything at leisure, since no one paid attention to him. Once brought out of hiding, the chief clerk took control of the conversation, as seemed to be his habit. The lawyer, whose initial weakness might have been intended only to drive away the new visitors, listened attentively with a hand to his ear. The uncle, acting as candle-bearer—he balanced the candle on his thigh, which the lawyer repeatedly watched with concern—soon lost his embarrassment and was merely delighted, both by the chief clerk's manner of speaking and by the gentle, wave-like hand movements accompanying it. K., leaning against the bedpost, was entirely neglected by the chief clerk, perhaps even deliberately, and served the older gentlemen only as an audience. Besides, he scarcely knew what was being discussed and thought now of the nurse and his uncle's poor treatment of her, now of whether he had seen the chief clerk before, perhaps even in the gathering at his first examination. Even if he was mistaken, the chief clerk would have fitted admirably among the people in the front row, the old gentlemen with sparse beards.

Then a crash from the entrance hall, like breaking china, made everyone listen. “I'll see what's happened,” said K., going out slowly, as though giving the others a chance to hold him back. Scarcely had he entered the hall and begun trying to find his way in the dark when a little hand, much smaller than his own, settled on the hand with which he still held the door and quietly closed it. It was the nurse, who had been waiting there. “Nothing's happened,” she whispered. “I only threw a plate against the wall to bring you out.” Embarrassed, K. said: “I was thinking about you too.” “All the better,” said the nurse. “Come.” After a few steps they reached a frosted-glass door, which she opened for him. “Do come in,” she said. This must have been the lawyer's study. As far as could be seen in the moonlight, which now brightly lit only a small square patch of floor at each of the two large windows, it was furnished with heavy old pieces. “Over here,” said the nurse, pointing to a dark chest with a carved wooden back. Even after sitting down, K. continued looking around. It was a large, high room; the poor people's lawyer's clients must have felt lost here. K. thought he could see the little steps with which visitors advanced towards the enormous desk. Then, however, he forgot it and had eyes only for the nurse, who sat very close beside him, almost pressing him against the armrest. “I thought,” she said, “you'd come out to me on your own, without my having to call you. It was strange. First you looked at me continually as soon as you came in, and then you left me waiting. Call me Leni, by the way,” she added quickly and abruptly, as though not a moment of this conversation should be wasted. “Gladly,” said K. “But as for what was strange, Leni, that's easily explained. First, I had to listen to the old gentlemen's chatter and couldn't run off for no reason; and second, I'm not forward but rather shy, and you certainly didn't look, Leni, as though you could be won in a single leap.” “That isn't it,” said Leni, laying her arm over the backrest and looking at K. “You didn't find me attractive, and you probably still don't.” “Attraction wouldn't amount to much,” K. said evasively. “Oh!” she said with a smile, gaining a certain superiority through K.'s remark and this little exclamation. K. therefore remained silent for a while. Having grown used to the darkness, he could distinguish various details of the furnishings. A large picture hanging to the right of the door particularly caught his attention, and he leaned forward to see it better. It showed a man in a judge's robes seated in a high throne-like chair, whose gilding stood out strongly in many places. The unusual thing was that the judge did not sit there calmly and with dignity, but pressed his left arm firmly against the back and side of the chair, while his right arm was entirely free, only his hand gripping the armrest, as though in the next moment he meant to spring up with a violent, perhaps indignant movement to say something decisive or even pronounce judgment. The accused was presumably to be imagined at the foot of the stairs, whose uppermost steps, covered by a yellow carpet, could still be seen in the picture. “Perhaps that's my judge,” said K., pointing at it. “I know him,” said Leni, looking up at the picture too. “He comes here often. The picture dates from his youth, but he can never have looked even remotely like it, because he's almost tiny. Yet he had himself stretched out like that in the picture, because he's insanely vain, like everyone here. But I'm vain too, and very unhappy that you don't find me attractive at all.” K. answered this last remark only by putting his arm around Leni and drawing her towards him. She quietly rested her head on his shoulder. To the rest, however, he said: “What rank does he hold?” “He's an examining magistrate,” she said, taking the hand with which K. held her and playing with his fingers. “Again only an examining magistrate,” said K., disappointed. “The senior officials hide themselves. But he's sitting on a throne.” “It's all invented,” said Leni, bending her face over K.'s hand. “In reality he sits on a kitchen chair with an old horse blanket folded on it. But must you keep thinking about your case?” she slowly added. “No, certainly not,” said K. “I probably even think about it too little.” “That isn't the mistake you're making,” said Leni. “You're too unyielding, so I've heard.” “Who said that?” K. asked, feeling her body against his chest and looking down at her thick, dark, tightly twisted hair. “I'd be giving away too much if I told you,” Leni replied. “Please don't ask for names, but correct your mistake. Don't be so unyielding any more. You can't defend yourself against this court; you have to confess. Do confess at the next opportunity. Only then is there a chance of slipping away, only then. Yet even that isn't possible without outside help. But you needn't worry about that help; I'll give it to you myself.” “You understand a great deal about this court and the deceits needed here,” said K., lifting her onto his lap because she was pressing too hard against him. “That's better,” she said, settling herself on his lap, smoothing her skirt and adjusting her blouse. Then she hung both hands around his neck, leaned back and looked at him for a long time. “And if I don't confess, you can't help me?” K. asked experimentally. I'm recruiting women to help me, he thought almost in surprise: first Miss Bürstner, then the court usher's wife, and finally this little nurse, who seems to have an incomprehensible need for me. The way she sits on my lap, as though it were the only proper place for her! “No,” Leni answered, slowly shaking her head. “Then I can't help you. But you don't want my help at all. It doesn't matter to you; you're stubborn and won't be persuaded.” “Do you have a lover?” she asked after a little while. “No,” said K. “Oh, yes,” she said. “Yes, actually,” said K. “Just think, I denied her, and yet I even carry her photograph with me.” At her request he showed her a photograph of Elsa. Curled up on his lap, she studied it. It was a snapshot, taken after one of the whirling dances Elsa liked to perform in the wine bar. Her skirt still flew around her in the folds of the turn; she had placed her hands on her firm hips and, her neck taut, was looking to the side with a laugh. The picture did not show whom she was laughing at. “She's tightly corseted,” said Leni, pointing to where she thought it could be seen. “I don't like her. She's clumsy and coarse. But perhaps she's gentle and kind to you; one could infer that from the picture. Big, strong girls like that often know nothing except how to be gentle and kind. But could she sacrifice herself for you?” “No,” said K. “She's neither gentle and kind, nor could she sacrifice herself for me. Nor have I asked either of her so far. In fact I haven't even looked at the picture as closely as you have.” “Then you don't care much about her,” said Leni. “So she isn't your lover at all.” “She is,” said K. “I won't take back what I said.” “Then let her be your lover for now,” said Leni. “But you wouldn't miss her much if you lost her or exchanged her for someone else—for me, for example.” “Certainly,” K. said with a smile. “That would be conceivable. But she has one great advantage over you: she knows nothing about my case, and even if she knew something, she wouldn't think about it. She wouldn't try to persuade me to give in.” “That's no advantage,” said Leni. “If she has no other advantages, I won't lose courage. Does she have any physical defect?” “A physical defect?” K. asked. “Yes,” said Leni. “I have a little defect like that myself. Look.” She spread the middle and ring fingers of her right hand apart; the connecting web of skin reached almost to the uppermost joint of the short fingers. In the dark K. did not at once see what she wanted to show him, so she guided his hand there for him to feel it. “What a trick of nature,” said K., adding, after examining the whole hand: “What a pretty claw!” With a kind of pride Leni watched K., in astonishment, repeatedly draw her two fingers apart and put them together, until finally he briefly kissed them and let go. “Oh!” she immediately exclaimed. “You kissed me!” Hurriedly, with her mouth open, she climbed on her knees onto his lap. K. looked up at her almost in dismay. Now that she was so close, a bitter, stimulating smell, like pepper, came from her. She drew his head to her, bent over him and bit and kissed his neck, even biting into his hair. “You've exchanged her for me,” she cried from time to time. “You see, now you have exchanged her for me!” Then her knee slipped; with a little cry she almost fell onto the carpet. K. put his arms around her to hold her up and was drawn down with her. “Now you belong to me,” she said.

“Here's the key to the house; come whenever you like,” were her last words, and as he left, an aimless kiss caught him on the back. A light rain was falling when he stepped out of the front door. He wanted to go into the middle of the street in the hope of catching sight of Leni at the window, when his uncle burst out of a car waiting in front of the house, which K. in his distraction had not noticed at all, seized him by the arms and pushed him against the doorway as though to pin him there. “Boy!” he cried. “How could you do that? You've done terrible harm to your case, which was going well. You creep away with a dirty little thing, who is moreover obviously the lawyer's mistress, and stay away for hours. You don't even look for an excuse, you hide nothing; no, quite openly you run to her and stay with her. And meanwhile we sit together: your uncle, wearing himself out for you; the lawyer, who is to be won over for you; and above all the chief clerk, that great man who practically controls your case at its present stage. We want to discuss how to help you. I have to handle the lawyer carefully, he in turn the chief clerk, and you had every reason at least to support me. Instead, you stay away. Eventually it can't be concealed. Well, they're polite, accomplished men; they don't mention it, they spare me, but in the end even they can no longer overcome it, and since they can't speak about the matter, they fall silent. We sat for minutes without a word, listening to see whether you might finally come. All in vain. At last the chief clerk, who has stayed much longer than he originally intended, gets up, takes his leave, visibly pities me without being able to help, waits a little longer at the door with incomprehensible kindness, and then goes. Naturally I was happy he had gone; I had already run out of air to breathe. It all affected the sick lawyer still more strongly. The good man couldn't speak at all when I took my leave of him. You've probably contributed to his complete collapse and are thus hastening the death of a man you depend on. And you leave me, your uncle, waiting here for hours in the rain. Just feel me—I'm soaked through.”

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: One winter morning—outside, snow was falling in the murky light—K. sat in his office, already extremely tired despite the early hour. To protect himself at least from the junior clerks, he had told the attendant to admit none of them, as he was occupied with a substantial piece of work. But instead of working he turned in his chair, slowly shifted a few objects about on the desk, then, without being aware of it, left his whole arm stretched out on the desktop and sat motionless, his head lowered.

The thought of the proceedings would no longer leave him. Several times already he had considered whether it would not be a good thing to draw up a written defence and submit it to the court. In it he intended to present a short account of his life and, for every event of any importance, explain his reasons for acting as he had, whether in his present judgement that way of acting was to be condemned or approved, and what reasons he could give for either conclusion. The advantages of such a written defence over merely being defended by the lawyer, who was not above criticism in other respects either, were beyond doubt. K. did not even know what the lawyer was doing; certainly it was not much, for a month now he had not summoned him, and at none of their earlier discussions had K. had the impression that this man could achieve much for him. Above all, he had asked him almost no questions. And there was so much to ask here. Questions were the main thing. K. felt as though he himself could ask all the questions needed here. The lawyer, however, instead of asking questions, did the talking himself or sat silently opposite him, bent a little forward over the desk, probably because his hearing was poor, pulled at a strand within his beard and looked down at the carpet, perhaps at the very place where K. had lain with Leni. Now and then he gave K. a few empty admonitions of the kind one gives children. Speeches as useless as they were boring, for which K. had no intention of paying a penny in the final reckoning. Once the lawyer thought he had humiliated him sufficiently, he generally began to cheer him up a little again. He had already, he would then say, won many similar cases, wholly or in part. Cases which, although in reality perhaps not as difficult as this one, had outwardly seemed still more hopeless. He had a list of these cases here in the drawer—at this he would tap some drawer of the desk—but unfortunately he could not show the papers, as these were official secrets. Nevertheless, the great experience he had acquired through all these cases was now benefiting K. He had of course begun work at once, and the first submission was already almost finished. It was very important, because the first impression made by the defence often determined the whole course of the proceedings. Unfortunately, though, he must draw K.'s attention to the fact that it sometimes happened that first submissions were not read at all in court. They were simply placed with the files, and it was pointed out that for the present, questioning and observing the accused was more important than anything written down. If the petitioner became insistent, they would add that before the decision, once all the material had been collected, all the documents would of course be examined together, including this first submission. Unfortunately, however, even this was generally untrue; the first submission was usually mislaid or lost altogether, and even if it was preserved until the end, it was scarcely read, as the lawyer had admittedly learnt only by hearsay. All this was regrettable, but not wholly unjustified. K. must not overlook the fact that the proceedings were not public; they could be made public if the court considered it necessary, but the law did not prescribe publicity. Consequently the court's documents, and above all the indictment, were inaccessible to the accused and his defence, so that in general one did not know, or at least did not know precisely, what the first submission ought to address, and thus it could really only contain anything relevant to the case by chance. Submissions that were truly pertinent and furnished evidence could only be drawn up later, when, in the course of the questioning of the accused, the individual charges and the grounds for them emerged more clearly or could be guessed at. Under these circumstances the defence was naturally in a very unfavourable and difficult position. But this too was intentional. Defence was not in fact permitted by law, but merely tolerated, and there was even disagreement as to whether the relevant passage in the law should be read as granting so much as toleration. Strictly speaking, therefore, there were no lawyers recognised by the court at all; all those who appeared before this court as lawyers were basically only backstreet lawyers. This naturally had a very degrading effect on the whole profession, and the next time K. went to the court offices he could take a look at the lawyers' room, just to have seen that too. He would probably be shocked by the company gathered there. The narrow, low-ceilinged chamber assigned to them alone showed the contempt the court had for these people. The chamber received light only through a small skylight, so high up that anyone wanting to look out—where, incidentally, the smoke from a chimney standing just in front drove into one's nose and blackened one's face—first had to find a colleague to take him on his back. In the floor of this chamber—to give just one more example of these conditions—there had for more than a year been a hole, not large enough for a person to fall through, but large enough for one's leg to sink into it completely. The lawyers' room was in the second attic; if anyone sank through, therefore, his leg hung down into the first attic, and directly into the corridor where the parties waited. It was no exaggeration when such conditions were called disgraceful in lawyers' circles. Complaints to the administration had not the slightest effect, yet the lawyers were strictly forbidden to have anything in the room altered at their own expense. But there were reasons for this treatment of the lawyers too. They wished to exclude the defence as far as possible; everything was to rest with the accused himself. Not a bad standpoint, essentially, but nothing would be more mistaken than to conclude from it that in this court lawyers were unnecessary for the accused. On the contrary, in no other court were they as necessary as in this one. The proceedings were generally kept secret not only from the public but also from the accused. Only as far as this was possible, of course, but it was possible to a very great extent. For the accused too had no access to the court documents, and it was very difficult to infer from the interrogations what the documents underlying them contained, particularly for the accused, who was after all involved in the matter and distracted by every kind of worry. This was where the defence intervened. Generally speaking, counsel were not allowed to be present at interrogations; they therefore had to question the accused about the interrogation afterwards, if possible while still at the door of the examining room, and extract from these accounts, often already very blurred, whatever was useful to the defence. But this was not the most important thing, since there was not much to be learnt in this way, though here, of course, as everywhere, a capable man learnt more than others. The most important thing remained the lawyer's personal connections; in these lay the chief value of the defence. Now K. had probably already gathered from his own experiences that the very lowest level of the court's organisation was not quite perfect, that it contained employees who neglected their duty and were open to bribery, which in a sense opened gaps in the court's strict isolation. This was where the majority of lawyers thrust their way in, where bribery and the wheedling out of information took place; indeed, at least in earlier times, there had even been cases of files being stolen. It could not be denied that in this way certain results, even surprisingly favourable ones, could be obtained for the accused for the moment, and these minor lawyers strutted about with them and attracted new clients, but for the further course of the case they meant either nothing or nothing good. Only honest personal connections had real value, and these must be with higher officials, by which of course only the higher officials of the lower ranks were meant. Only in this way could the progress of the proceedings be influenced, imperceptibly at first, admittedly, but later more and more clearly. Naturally only a few lawyers could do this, and in this respect K.'s choice had been very fortunate. Perhaps only one or two other lawyers could point to connections comparable to Dr Huld's. These men, however, took no interest in the company in the lawyers' room and had nothing to do with it. All the closer, though, was their connection with the court officials. It was not even always necessary for Dr Huld to go to court, wait in the examining magistrates' anterooms for them to happen to appear, and according to their mood obtain a success that was usually only apparent, or not even that. No, K. had seen it himself: the officials, including quite senior ones, came of their own accord, willingly supplied information, openly or at least in terms easy to interpret, discussed the next stages of cases, indeed in individual instances even allowed themselves to be persuaded and readily accepted another's view. Admittedly one must not trust them too far precisely in this last respect; however firmly they stated their new intention, favourable to the defence, they might still go straight to their office and issue a court decision for the following day that contained the exact opposite and was perhaps much harsher for the accused than their original intention, which they claimed to have abandoned completely. Naturally there was no way of countering this, for what they had said in private had, after all, only been said in private and allowed no public consequences to be drawn from it, even if the defence were not otherwise obliged to strive to retain these gentlemen's favour. On the other hand it was certainly also true that the gentlemen did not make contact with the defence—only with an expert defence, naturally—simply out of love of humanity or friendly feelings; rather, in a certain respect, they depended on it. Here the disadvantage of a judicial organisation that prescribed secret reporting even at its beginnings made itself felt. The officials lacked contact with the population; they were well equipped for the ordinary, average cases, which rolled along their course almost of their own accord and needed only a push here and there, but faced with the quite simple cases, as also with the particularly difficult ones, they were often at a loss, for, hemmed in by their law day and night, they lacked a proper sense of human relationships, and in such cases they sorely missed it. Then they came to the lawyer for advice, and behind them an attendant carried the files which were otherwise so secret. At this window one could have come across many gentlemen, of whom one would least have expected it, looking down into the street in utter desolation while the lawyer studied the files at his desk in order to be able to give them sound advice. Incidentally, it was precisely on such occasions that one could see how extraordinarily seriously the gentlemen took their profession, and how they fell into deep despair over obstacles which by their nature they could not overcome. Their position was not easy in other respects either, and one must not do them an injustice by considering it easy. The hierarchy and ascending ranks of the court were infinite and beyond the view even of the initiated. But proceedings before the courts were generally secret even from the lower officials, so that they could hardly ever follow the matters they dealt with completely through their later course; a case thus appeared within their jurisdiction, often without their knowing where it came from, and passed on without their learning where it went. The lessons that could be drawn from studying the individual stages of a case, the final decision and its grounds were therefore lost to these officials. They were allowed to concern themselves only with the portion of the proceedings that the law marked out for them, and of what followed, hence of the results of their own work, they generally knew less than the defence, which as a rule remained in contact with the accused almost to the end of the proceedings. In this respect too, therefore, they could learn much of value from the defence. Bearing all this in mind, could K. still wonder at the irritability of the officials, which sometimes expressed itself towards the parties in a manner—everyone experienced this—that was insulting? All the officials were irritable, even when they seemed calm. The minor lawyers naturally had to suffer particularly much from it. The following story, for example, was told, and had every appearance of being true. An old official, a good, quiet gentleman, had spent a day and a night continuously studying a difficult case which had become especially complicated through the lawyer's submissions—these officials really were more industrious than anyone else. Towards morning, after twenty-four hours of probably not very fruitful work, he went to the entrance, lay in wait there and threw every lawyer who tried to enter down the stairs. The lawyers gathered on the landing below and discussed what they should do; on the one hand they had no actual right to be admitted, so that legally they could scarcely take any action against the official, and, as already mentioned, they also had to take care not to turn the body of officials against them. On the other hand, every day not spent at court was lost to them, and it was therefore very important to them to get in. Finally they agreed to tire the old gentleman out. Again and again a lawyer was sent up, ran up the stairs and then, offering as much resistance as possible, though admittedly passive resistance, allowed himself to be thrown down, where his colleagues caught him. This went on for about an hour, then the old gentleman, who was already exhausted by his night's work, really did grow tired and went back to his office. At first those below would not believe it, and sent one of their number ahead to look behind the door and see whether it really was clear. Only then did they enter, and probably did not even dare to grumble. For the lawyers—and even the smallest of them could after all comprehend the circumstances at least in part—were entirely without any desire to introduce or enforce improvements at the court, whereas—and this was very characteristic—almost every accused person, even quite simple-minded people, began thinking of proposals for improvement as soon as they first entered the proceedings, and often wasted time and energy on them that could have been put to much better use elsewhere. The only right thing was to accept the existing conditions. Even if it were possible to improve individual details—but this was a senseless superstition—one would at best have achieved something for future cases, while doing oneself immeasurable harm by attracting the particular attention of the invariably vindictive body of officials. Above all, attract no attention! Keep quiet, however much it went against one's grain! Try to understand that this great judicial organism remained, in a sense, forever in suspension, and that if one independently changed something in one's own place, one indeed removed the ground beneath one's feet and might fall, while the great organism easily compensated for the small disturbance in some other place—everything was connected, after all—and remained unchanged, unless indeed, as was even probable, it grew still more tightly knit, still more vigilant, still stricter, still more malicious. One should leave the work to the lawyer instead of disrupting it. Reproaches were not much use, particularly if one could not make the reason for them understood in its full significance, but it must nevertheless be said how much harm K. had done his case through his behaviour towards the chief clerk. This influential man could almost be struck off the list of those through whom anything could be done for K. He ignored even passing references to the proceedings with obvious deliberation. In some things the officials were like children. Often they could be so hurt by harmless things, among which K.'s behaviour unfortunately did not belong, that they stopped talking even to good friends, turned away when they met them and worked against them in every possible way. Then one day, surprisingly, for no particular reason, a small joke which one only ventured because everything seemed hopeless would make them laugh, and they were reconciled. It was at once difficult and easy to deal with them; there were scarcely any principles for doing so. Sometimes it was a wonder that a single ordinary lifetime sufficed to grasp enough to be able to work here with some success. There were, admittedly, gloomy hours, such as everyone had, when one believed one had achieved nothing at all, when it seemed that only those cases which were destined for a good outcome from the beginning had ended well, as they would have done without assistance, while all the others had been lost, despite all the running alongside them, all the effort, all the little apparent successes which had caused such delight. Then, indeed, nothing seemed certain any longer, and in answer to particular questions one would not even venture to deny that one's assistance had actually led astray cases which by their nature were going well. That too was a kind of self-confidence, but it was the only kind left then. Lawyers were particularly exposed to such attacks—which were only attacks, of course, nothing more—when a case they had brought far enough and satisfactorily along was suddenly taken out of their hands. That was probably the worst thing that could happen to a lawyer. It was not the accused who took the case away from them; that probably never happened, an accused man who had once engaged a particular lawyer had to stay with him, whatever happened. How could he possibly hold his own alone once he had sought help? That did not happen, then, but what did sometimes happen was that the proceedings took a direction in which the lawyer was no longer allowed to follow. The case and the accused and everything were simply removed from the lawyer; then even the best connections with the officials could no longer help, for they themselves knew nothing. The proceedings had simply entered a stage at which no further help might be given, at which inaccessible courts dealt with them, at which even the accused could no longer be reached by the lawyer. Then one day one came home and found on one's desk all the many submissions one had made in this case with such diligence and such fine hopes; they had been returned because they could not be carried over into the new stage of the proceedings, they were worthless scraps. Yet the case need not be lost, not at all, at least there was no decisive reason for supposing so; one merely knew nothing more of the case and would learn nothing more of it either. Fortunately, such cases were exceptions, and even if K.'s case should prove to be one of them, it was still a long way from such a stage for the present. There was still ample opportunity here for a lawyer's work, and K. could be certain it was being used. As mentioned, the submission had not yet been handed in, but there was no hurry about that; much more important were the preliminary discussions with influential officials, and these had already taken place. With varying success, as should frankly be admitted. It was much better not to disclose details for the present, which might only affect K. unfavourably and make him either too hopeful or too fearful; let it merely be said that some had spoken very favourably and shown themselves very willing, while others had expressed themselves less favourably but had by no means refused their assistance. Thus the result as a whole was very gratifying, only one must draw no particular conclusions from it, since all preliminary negotiations began in much the same way and only their subsequent development showed their value. In any case nothing had yet been lost, and if it should still prove possible to win over the chief clerk despite everything—various steps had already been taken to this end—then the whole thing would be, as surgeons put it, a clean wound, and one could confidently await what followed.

The lawyer was inexhaustible in speeches of this kind and others like them. They were repeated at every visit. There was always progress, but the nature of that progress could never be disclosed. Work on the first submission continued all the time, but it was not finished, which generally proved at the next visit to have been something of an advantage, since the recent period, as could not have been foreseen, would have been a very unfavourable one for handing it in. If K., quite worn out by the speeches, sometimes remarked that even allowing for all the difficulties, things were moving very slowly, he was told that they were not moving slowly at all, though they would have been much further along already if K. had turned to the lawyer in good time. Unfortunately he had failed to do that, and this failure would bring further disadvantages too, not merely delays.

The only welcome interruption of these visits was Leni, who always managed to arrange things so that she brought the lawyer his tea while K. was present. Then she stood behind K., apparently watching as the lawyer, bending low over his cup with a kind of greed, poured out and drank his tea, and secretly allowed K. to take her hand. There was complete silence. The lawyer drank, K. pressed Leni's hand, and Leni sometimes ventured to stroke K.'s hair gently. “Are you still here?” the lawyer asked when he had finished. “I wanted to take the things away,” Leni said; there was one last pressure of the hand, the lawyer wiped his mouth and began talking at K. with renewed vigour.

Was it comfort or despair that the lawyer wanted to produce? K. did not know, but he soon took it as certain that his defence was not in good hands. Everything the lawyer said might be correct, although it was transparent that he wanted to put himself in the foreground as much as possible, and had probably never conducted so great a case as, in his opinion, K.'s was. But the personal connections with the officials, stressed incessantly, remained suspicious. Must they be exploited exclusively for K.'s benefit? The lawyer never forgot to point out that these were only lower officials, officials in a very dependent position, whose advancement might probably be affected by certain turns taken by the proceedings. Were they perhaps using the lawyer to bring about such turns, naturally always unfavourable to the accused? Perhaps they did not do this in every case; certainly, that was unlikely, and there were probably other cases in the course of which they granted the lawyer advantages in return for his services, since they too must be concerned to preserve his reputation intact. But if this was indeed how matters stood, in what way would they intervene in K.'s case, which, as the lawyer explained, was a very difficult and therefore important one, and had attracted great attention at the court from the very beginning? There could be little doubt what they would do. One could already see signs of it in the fact that the first submission had still not been handed in, although the proceedings had lasted for months, and that according to the lawyer's statements everything was still at its beginnings, which was naturally very well suited to lulling the accused to sleep and keeping him helpless, so as suddenly to assail him with the decision, or at least with the announcement that the investigation, concluded to his disadvantage, was being passed on to the higher authorities.

It was absolutely necessary for K. to intervene himself. Precisely in states of great fatigue, as on this winter morning, when everything drifted through his mind without his volition, this conviction was irresistible. The contempt he had formerly felt for the proceedings no longer held. Had he been alone in the world, he could easily have disregarded the proceedings, although it was also certain that in that case they would never have arisen at all. But now his uncle had already dragged him to the lawyer, family considerations had a say; his position was no longer entirely independent of the course of the proceedings, he himself had imprudently mentioned them to acquaintances with a certain inexplicable satisfaction, others had learnt of them in unknown ways, his relationship with Miss Bürstner seemed to fluctuate in accordance with the proceedings—in short, he scarcely had a choice any longer whether to accept or reject them, he stood in their midst and had to defend himself. If he was tired, then things were bad.

For the present, however, there was no reason for excessive concern. He had managed to work his way up to his high position at the bank in a comparatively short time and to maintain himself there with everyone's recognition; he needed now only to turn a little of the abilities that had made this possible towards the proceedings, and there was no doubt that they must end well. Above all, if anything was to be achieved, it was necessary to reject from the outset every thought of possible guilt. There was no guilt. The proceedings were nothing but a large business transaction, such as he had often concluded to the bank's advantage, a transaction within which, as was the rule, various dangers lurked that simply had to be warded off. For this purpose, admittedly, one must not toy with thoughts of any guilt, but hold as firmly as possible to the thought of one's own advantage. From this point of view it was also unavoidable that he should withdraw his representation from the lawyer very soon, preferably that very evening. According to the lawyer's accounts this was admittedly unheard of and probably deeply insulting, but K. could not tolerate his efforts in the proceedings meeting obstacles that might have been created by his own lawyer. Once the lawyer had been shaken off, however, the submission must be handed in at once, and pressure applied, if possible every day, for it to be considered. For this purpose it would naturally not be enough for K. to sit in the corridor like the others and put his hat under the bench. He himself, or the women, or other messengers, must besiege the officials day after day and force them, instead of looking out through the grille into the corridor, to sit down at their desks and study K.'s submission. There must be no relaxing of these efforts, everything must be organised and supervised; for once the court should come up against an accused man who knew how to uphold his rights.

But although K. felt capable of carrying all this out, the difficulty of composing the submission was overwhelming. Earlier, even a week ago perhaps, he had been able to think only with shame that he might one day be obliged to make such a submission himself; that it could also be difficult had not occurred to him at all. He remembered how one morning, when he was overwhelmed with work, he had suddenly pushed everything aside and taken out his writing pad to try drafting the line of thought for such a submission and perhaps place it at the disposal of the ponderous lawyer, and how at that very moment the door of the manager's office had opened and the deputy manager had come in laughing heartily. It had been very embarrassing for K. at the time, although the deputy manager had of course not been laughing at the submission, of which he knew nothing, but at a stock-exchange joke he had just heard, a joke which required a drawing to be understood, and which the deputy manager now made, bending over K.'s desk, with K.'s pencil, which he took from his hand, on the pad intended for the submission.

Today K. knew nothing of shame any more; the submission had to be made. If he could find no time for it at the office, which was very likely, then he must do it at home at night. If the nights proved insufficient too, then he must take leave. Only do not stop halfway; that was the most senseless thing, not merely in business but always and everywhere. Admittedly, the submission meant almost endless work. One need not have a particularly anxious disposition to come easily to believe that it was impossible ever to finish the submission. Not through laziness or guile, which alone could prevent the lawyer from finishing it, but because, in ignorance of the existing charge and still more of its possible extensions, the whole of one's life, down to its smallest actions and events, had to be recalled, set out and examined from every side. And what a dismal task it was besides. It might be suitable some day after retirement for occupying a mind grown childish and helping it get through the long days. But now, when K. needed all his thoughts for his work, when every hour passed at the greatest speed, since he was still rising and already constituted a threat to the deputy manager, and when as a young man he wanted to enjoy the short evenings and nights, now he was to begin composing this submission. Once again his thinking ended in complaints. Almost involuntarily, merely to put an end to this, he felt with his finger for the button of the electric bell that rang in the anteroom. As he pressed it he looked up at the clock. It was eleven; he had dreamed away two hours, a long and precious time, and was naturally still more exhausted than before. Nevertheless, the time was not wasted; he had made decisions that might be valuable. Besides various items of post, the attendants brought two visiting cards from gentlemen who had already been waiting for K. for some time. These happened to be very important clients of the bank, who really should not have been kept waiting under any circumstances. Why did they come at such an inconvenient time?—and why, the gentlemen behind the closed door in their turn seemed to ask, did the industrious K. use the best business hours for private affairs? Tired from what had gone before and tired in anticipation of what was to follow, K. rose to receive the first.

He was a small, lively gentleman, a manufacturer whom K. knew well. He regretted disturbing K. in important work, and K. in turn regretted having kept the manufacturer waiting so long. But even this expression of regret he delivered so mechanically and with almost the wrong emphasis that the manufacturer must have noticed it if he had not been wholly absorbed in the business matter. Instead he hurriedly drew bills and tables from every pocket, spread them out before K., explained various items, corrected a small error in calculation that he had noticed even in this cursory survey, reminded K. of a similar transaction he had concluded with him about a year ago, mentioned in passing that this time another bank was making the greatest sacrifices to compete for the business, and finally fell silent to hear K.'s opinion. At first K. had indeed followed the manufacturer's speech closely; the thought of the important transaction had caught hold of him too, but unfortunately not for long, he had soon ceased listening, then for a little while had still nodded at the manufacturer's louder exclamations, but finally had given that up too and confined himself to looking at the bald head bent over the papers and wondering when the manufacturer would at last realise that his whole speech was useless. When he now fell silent, K. really thought at first that he was doing so to give him the opportunity to admit that he was incapable of listening. Only with regret did he realise, from the intent gaze of the manufacturer, evidently prepared for every objection, that the business discussion must continue. He therefore bowed his head as though before an order and began slowly moving his pencil back and forth over the papers; here and there he paused and stared at a figure. The manufacturer suspected objections; perhaps the figures really were not fixed, perhaps they were not the decisive thing, at any rate he covered the papers with his hand and, moving very close to K., began a general account of the transaction once more. “It's difficult,” K. said, pursing his lips, and, since the papers, the only tangible thing, were covered, he sank helplessly against the armrest. He looked up only faintly even when the door of the manager's office opened and the deputy manager appeared there, not quite distinctly, as though behind a gauze veil. K. gave this no further thought, but followed only its immediate effect, which was very welcome to him. For the manufacturer at once hopped up from his chair and hurried towards the deputy manager, but K. would have liked to make him ten times quicker still, for he feared the deputy manager might disappear again. It was a needless fear; the gentlemen met, shook hands and came together towards K.'s desk. The manufacturer complained that he had found so little inclination towards the transaction in the authorised signatory, and pointed to K., who bent over the papers again under the deputy manager's gaze. Then, as the two leaned against the desk and the manufacturer set about winning the deputy manager over, K. felt as though two men, whose stature he imagined exaggeratedly, were negotiating about him over his head. Slowly, with his eyes cautiously turned upwards, he tried to discover what was happening above, took one of the papers from the desk without looking, laid it on his flat hand and gradually raised it towards the gentlemen as he himself stood up. He had no definite thought in doing this, but acted only in the feeling that this was how he must behave once he had finished the great submission which was to exonerate him completely. The deputy manager, who was taking part in the conversation with full attention, only glanced fleetingly at the paper, did not read what was written there at all, for what mattered to the authorised signatory did not matter to him, took it from K.'s hand, said, “Thank you, I know all about it,” and calmly laid it back on the desk. K. looked at him bitterly from the side. But the deputy manager did not notice at all, or, if he did, was only encouraged by it, laughed aloud several times, once caused the manufacturer obvious embarrassment with a quick-witted reply, from which he immediately rescued him by raising an objection to his own argument, and finally invited him to come over to his office, where they could bring the matter to a conclusion. “It's a very important matter,” he said to the manufacturer, “I see that perfectly. And our authorised signatory”—even with this remark he was really addressing only the manufacturer—“will certainly be glad if we take it off his hands. The matter calls for calm consideration. But he seems very overburdened today; besides, several people in the anteroom have been waiting for him for hours.” K. had just enough composure left to turn away from the deputy manager and direct his friendly but rigid smile only at the manufacturer; otherwise he did not intervene at all, but leaned a little forward with both hands braced on the desk like a shop assistant behind a counter, and watched the two gentlemen, still talking, take the papers from the desk and disappear into the manager's office. In the doorway the manufacturer turned round once more and said he was not taking his leave yet, but would of course report the result of the discussion to the authorised signatory; he also had another small piece of information for him.

At last K. was alone. It did not occur to him to admit any other client, and he was only dimly aware how pleasant it was that the people outside believed he was still negotiating with the manufacturer, and that for this reason no one, not even the attendant, could come in. He went to the window, sat on the sill, held on to the handle with one hand and looked out over the square. The snow was still falling; it had not grown any brighter at all.

He sat like this for a long time, without knowing what was really troubling him, only now and then looking a little alarmedly over his shoulder towards the anteroom door, where he had mistakenly thought he heard a sound. But since no one came, he grew calmer, went to the washstand, washed himself with cold water and returned with a clearer head to his place by the window. The decision to take his defence into his own hands now presented itself as more serious than he had originally supposed. As long as he had shifted the defence on to the lawyer, he had after all remained fundamentally little affected by the proceedings; he had observed them from a distance and could scarcely be reached by them directly, he had been able to look and see how his case stood whenever he wanted, but he had also been able to draw his head back whenever he wanted. Now, however, if he conducted his defence himself, he must, at least for the moment, expose himself wholly and entirely to the court; the result of this was indeed to be his complete and final liberation later, but to achieve that he must for the present put himself in far greater danger than before. Had he wanted to doubt it, today's encounter with the deputy manager and the manufacturer could have convinced him sufficiently of the contrary. How he had sat there, already completely dazed by the mere decision to defend himself! But what would it be like later? What days lay ahead of him! Would he find the path that led through everything to a good end? Did not a careful defence—and anything else was pointless—did not a careful defence mean at the same time the necessity of shutting himself off from everything else as far as possible? Would he get through it safely? And how was he to manage it at the bank? It was not merely a question of the submission, for which a period of leave might perhaps have sufficed, although asking for leave just now would have been a great risk; it was a question of an entire case whose duration could not be foreseen. What an obstacle had suddenly been thrown into K.'s career!

And now he was supposed to work for the bank?—He looked towards the desk.—Now he was supposed to admit clients and negotiate with them? While his proceedings rolled on, while up in the attic the court officials sat over the papers in his case, he was to attend to the bank's business? Did it not look like a torture which, sanctioned by the court, was connected with the proceedings and accompanied them? And would the bank perhaps take his particular situation into account when judging his work? No one would, ever. His case was not entirely unknown, although it was not yet quite clear who knew of it and how much. But hopefully the rumour had not yet reached the deputy manager, otherwise one would already have had to see plainly how he would exploit it against K., without any collegiality or humanity. And the manager? Certainly, he was well disposed towards K., and as soon as he learnt of the proceedings he would probably have wanted, as far as lay in his power, to make various things easier for K., but he would certainly not have succeeded, for now that the counterweight K. had hitherto provided was beginning to weaken, he was falling more and more under the influence of the deputy manager, who was also exploiting the manager's ailing condition to strengthen his own power. What, then, had K. to hope for? Perhaps such reflections weakened his powers of resistance, but it was also necessary not to deceive himself and to see everything as clearly as was possible at present.

For no particular reason, merely to avoid having to return to the desk yet, he opened the window. It was difficult to open; he had to turn the handle with both hands. Then fog mingled with smoke drew into the room through the whole width and height of the window and filled it with a slight smell of burning. A few snowflakes were blown in too. “An unpleasant autumn,” said the manufacturer behind K.; returning from the deputy manager, he had entered the room unnoticed. K. nodded and looked uneasily at the manufacturer's briefcase, from which he would presumably now take the papers to tell K. the result of his negotiations with the deputy manager. But the manufacturer followed K.'s gaze, tapped his briefcase and said without opening it: “You want to hear how it turned out. I've practically got the completed deal in my bag. A charming man, your deputy manager, but by no means harmless.” He laughed, shook K.'s hand and tried to make him laugh too. But now K. again found it suspicious that the manufacturer did not want to show him the papers, and he found nothing to laugh at in his remark. “Mr K.,” the manufacturer said, “the weather must be affecting you. You look so depressed today.” “Yes,” K. said, putting his hand to his temple, “headaches, family worries.” “Quite right,” said the manufacturer, who was a hurried man and could never listen to anyone patiently, “everyone has his cross to bear.” Involuntarily K. had taken a step towards the door, as though to see the manufacturer out, but the latter said: “I have one more small piece of information for you, Mr K. I'm very much afraid I may be troubling you with it today of all days, but I've already been to see you twice recently and forgotten it each time. If I put it off any longer, though, it will probably lose its purpose altogether. That would be a pity, because at bottom what I have to tell you may not be without value.” Before K. had time to reply, the manufacturer stepped close to him, tapped his chest lightly with his knuckle and said softly: “You have a case against you, don't you?” K. stepped back and immediately exclaimed: “The deputy manager told you that.” “Oh no,” said the manufacturer, “how would the deputy manager know?” “Through you?” K. asked, much more composed already. “Now and then I hear something about the court,” said the manufacturer, “and that has to do with what I wanted to tell you.” “So many people have connections with the court!” K. said, his head lowered, and led the manufacturer to the desk. They sat down again as before, and the manufacturer said: “Unfortunately there isn't very much I can tell you. But in such matters one shouldn't neglect even the smallest thing. Besides, I felt the need to help you somehow, however modest my help might be. We've been good business friends until now, haven't we?
