Well then.” K. wanted to apologise for his behaviour during their discussion today, but the manufacturer allowed no interruption, tucked the briefcase high under his arm to show he was in a hurry, and went on: “I know about your case through a certain Titorelli. He's a painter; Titorelli is only his professional name, I don't know his real name at all. For years now he's been coming to my office from time to time, bringing little pictures for which I always give him a sort of alms—he's practically a beggar. They're pretty pictures, incidentally, heath landscapes and that sort of thing. These sales—we had both grown used to them—went off quite smoothly. But once these visits came too frequently after all, I reproached him, we got into conversation, I was interested in how he could support himself by painting alone, and then, to my astonishment, I learnt that his main source of income was portrait painting. He worked for the court, he said. Which court, I asked. And then he told me about the court. You will probably be best able to imagine how astonished I was by these accounts. Since then, on each of his visits I hear some news of the court, and so little by little I gain considerable insight into the matter. Admittedly Titorelli is talkative, and I often have to fend him off, not only because he certainly tells lies too, but above all because a businessman like me, almost collapsing under his own business worries, can't concern himself much with other people's affairs as well. But that's by the way. Perhaps, I thought just now, Titorelli can be of a little help to you; he knows many judges, and even if he doesn't have much influence himself, he can still give you advice on how to approach various influential people. And even if this advice isn't in itself decisive, in your possession it will nevertheless, I believe, be of great significance. You're practically a lawyer yourself. I always say: K., the authorised signatory, is practically a lawyer. Oh, I'm not worried about your case. But will you go to Titorelli now? With my recommendation he'll certainly do everything he can. I really think you ought to go. It needn't be today, of course; some time, when the opportunity arises. Admittedly—and I want to add this—the fact that it is I who give you this advice doesn't oblige you in the least actually to visit Titorelli. No, if you think you can do without Titorelli, it is certainly better to leave him out of it altogether. Perhaps you already have a quite definite plan, and Titorelli might disrupt it. No, in that case naturally don't go under any circumstances. It certainly takes some effort to accept advice from a fellow like that. Well, as you please. Here is the letter of introduction, and here is the address.”

Disappointed, K. took the letter and put it in his pocket. Even in the most favourable case, the benefit the recommendation could bring him was comparatively smaller than the harm in the manufacturer's knowing about his proceedings and the painter spreading the news further. He could scarcely force himself to thank the manufacturer, who was already on his way to the door, in a few words. “I'll go,” he said as he took leave of him at the door, “or, since I'm very busy at present, write and ask him to come to my office some time.” “I knew,” said the manufacturer, “that you'd find the best way out. Admittedly, I thought you would prefer to avoid inviting people like this Titorelli to the bank to talk to him here about the proceedings. Nor is it always advantageous to let letters to such people out of one's hands. But I'm sure you've thought it all through and know what you can do.” K. nodded and accompanied the manufacturer through the anteroom as well. But despite his outward calm he was deeply alarmed at himself. He had really only said he would write to Titorelli to show the manufacturer somehow that he valued the recommendation and was immediately considering the possibilities of meeting Titorelli, but if he had considered Titorelli's assistance valuable, he would not have hesitated actually to write to him. Yet he had recognised the dangers this might entail only through the manufacturer's remark. Could he really rely so little on his own judgement already? If it was possible for him to invite a dubious person to the bank in an explicit letter, in order to ask his advice about the proceedings with only a door separating him from the deputy manager, was it not possible, and even very likely, that he overlooked other dangers too, or ran straight into them? There would not always be someone beside him to warn him. And just now, when he intended to act with his powers collected, doubts of this kind, hitherto unknown to him, about his own vigilance had to arise! Were the difficulties he felt in carrying out his office work now to begin in the proceedings too? Now, however, he could no longer understand at all how it had been possible for him to want to write to Titorelli and invite him to the bank.

He was still shaking his head over it when the attendant stepped to his side and drew his attention to three gentlemen sitting on a bench here in the anteroom. They had been waiting a long time to be admitted to K. Now, as the attendant spoke to K., they had stood up, and each wanted to seize a favourable opportunity to approach K. before the others. Since the bank had been so inconsiderate as to let them waste their time here in the waiting room, they too would show no more consideration. “Mr K.,” one of them was already saying. But K. had asked the attendant to bring his winter coat, and as he put it on with the attendant's help he said to all three: “Forgive me, gentlemen, unfortunately I have no time to receive you at the moment. I do beg your pardon, but I have an urgent business errand to attend to and must leave at once. You yourselves have seen how long I've just been held up. Would you be so kind as to return tomorrow, or whenever suits you? Or perhaps we could discuss the matters by telephone? Or perhaps you'd care to tell me briefly now what they concern, and I'll give you a detailed written answer. The best thing, though, would be for you to come again soon.” These proposals of K.'s so astonished the gentlemen, who were now to have waited completely in vain, that they looked at one another in silence. “Then we're agreed?” asked K., who had turned towards the attendant, now bringing his hat as well. Through the open door of K.'s office one could see that the snowfall outside had grown much heavier. K. therefore turned up his coat collar and buttoned it high under his throat.

Just then the deputy manager came out of the adjoining room, smiled as he saw K. in his winter coat negotiating with the gentlemen, and asked: “You're leaving now, Mr K.?” “Yes,” K. said, straightening up, “I have a business errand to attend to.” But the deputy manager had already turned to the gentlemen. “And these gentlemen?” he asked. “I believe they've been waiting a long time.” “We've already reached an agreement,” K. said. But now the gentlemen could no longer be restrained; they surrounded K. and declared that they would not have waited for hours if their affairs were not important and did not need to be discussed now, at length and in private. The deputy manager listened to them for a little while, also looked at K., who held his hat in his hand and was removing dust from it here and there, and then said: “Gentlemen, there is a very simple way out. If you will make do with me, I shall be very happy to conduct the discussions in Mr K.'s place. Your affairs must of course be discussed at once. We are businessmen like yourselves, and know how to value businessmen's time properly. Would you care to come in here?” And he opened the door leading to the anteroom of his office.

How well the deputy manager knew how to appropriate everything K. was now obliged to give up! But was K. not giving up more than was absolutely necessary? While he ran off with vague and, as he had to admit, very slight hopes to an unknown painter, his standing here was suffering irreparable damage. It would probably have been far better to take off his winter coat again and at least win back for himself the two gentlemen who would still have to wait next door. K. might have tried it, too, if he had not now caught sight of the deputy manager in his room, searching for something in the bookstand as though it were his own. As K. approached the door in agitation, he called: “Oh, you haven't left yet.” He turned his face towards him, its many taut lines seeming to bear witness to strength rather than age, and immediately began searching again. “I'm looking for a copy of a contract,” he said, “which, according to the firm's representative, should be with you. Would you help me look?” K. took a step, but the deputy manager said: “Thank you, I've found it,” and returned to his own room with a large bundle of papers containing not only the copy of the contract but certainly a great deal else as well.

At present I'm no match for him, K. told himself, but once my personal difficulties have been cleared away, he shall indeed be the first to feel it, and as bitterly as possible. Somewhat calmed by this thought, K. instructed the attendant, who had long been holding the door to the corridor open for him, to inform the manager when the opportunity arose that he was out on a business errand, and left the bank almost happy at being able to devote himself more completely to his own affair for a while.

He drove straight to the painter, who lived in a suburb at the opposite end of the city from the one where the court offices were situated. It was a poorer neighbourhood still, the houses darker still, the streets full of filth drifting slowly about on the melted snow. At the house where the painter lived, only one leaf of the large gateway was open, while beneath the other a gap had been broken in the masonry, from which, just as K. approached, a disgusting yellow, steaming liquid shot out, sending a rat scurrying into the nearby drain. At the foot of the stairs a small child lay face down on the ground and cried, but it could scarcely be heard because of the noise, drowning everything out, that came from a tinsmith's workshop on the other side of the entrance passage. The workshop door was open; three assistants stood in a semicircle round some piece of work, striking it with hammers. A large sheet of tinplate hanging on the wall cast a pale light which came through between two of the assistants and lit up their faces and work aprons. K. gave everything only a fleeting glance; he wanted to finish here as quickly as possible, merely sound out the painter in a few words and return to the bank at once. If he had even the smallest success here, it should still have a good effect on his work at the bank today. On the third floor he had to slow his pace; he was quite out of breath, the stairs, like the storeys, were excessively high, and the painter was supposed to live right at the top in an attic room. The air too was very oppressive; there was no open stairwell, the narrow staircase was enclosed on both sides by walls in which only here and there, almost right at the top, small windows had been set. Just as K. paused for a moment, a few little girls ran out of a flat and hurried laughing further up the stairs. K. followed them slowly, caught up with one of the girls who had stumbled and fallen behind the others, and, as they continued climbing side by side, asked her: “Does a painter called Titorelli live here?” The girl, scarcely thirteen and slightly hunchbacked, nudged him with her elbow at this and looked up at him sideways. Neither her youth nor her physical deformity had prevented her from being thoroughly corrupted already. She did not even smile, but looked at K. gravely, with a sharp, inviting gaze. K. pretended not to have noticed her behaviour and asked: “Do you know the painter Titorelli?” She nodded and asked in turn: “What do you want with him?” K. thought it might be useful to find out a little about Titorelli quickly: “I want him to paint me,” he said. “Paint you?” she asked, opening her mouth excessively wide, striking K. lightly with her hand as though he had said something extraordinarily surprising or awkward, lifting her already very short skirt with both hands and running as fast as she could after the other girls, whose shouts were already fading indistinctly above. At the next turn of the stairs, however, K. found all the girls again. The hunchback had evidently told them of K.'s intention, and they were waiting for him. They stood on either side of the stairs, pressing against the wall so that K. could pass comfortably between them, and smoothed their aprons with their hands. All their faces, like this formation in two rows, presented a mixture of childishness and depravity. At the head of the girls, who now closed up behind K. laughing, was the hunchback, who took the lead. K. owed it to her that he immediately found the right way. He had been about to continue straight up, but she showed him that he must take a branch of the stairs to reach Titorelli. The staircase leading to him was particularly narrow, very long, without a bend, visible for its entire length and ending directly at Titorelli's door. This door, which unlike the rest of the stairs was comparatively brightly lit by a small fanlight set crookedly above it, was made of unpainted timbers, on which the name Titorelli had been painted in broad strokes of red. K. and his following were scarcely halfway up the stairs when the door above, evidently in response to the sound of so many feet, opened a little and a man, probably wearing only a nightshirt, appeared in the gap. “Oh!” he cried when he saw the crowd approaching, and disappeared. The hunchback clapped her hands with delight, and the other girls pressed behind K. to drive him forward more quickly.

But they had not even reached the top when the painter flung the door wide open and invited K. to enter with a deep bow. The girls, however, he warded off; he would let none of them in, however much they begged and however hard they tried to force their way in, against his will if they could not do so with his permission. Only the hunchback managed to slip under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, seized her by her skirts, whirled her once round himself and then set her down outside the door with the other girls, who, even while the painter had left his post, had not dared cross the threshold. K. did not know what to make of it all, for it seemed as though everything were happening by friendly agreement. One after another the girls at the door craned their necks, called out various words to the painter, intended as jokes, which K. did not understand, and the painter too laughed while the hunchback almost flew in his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed once more to K., held out his hand and introduced himself: “Titorelli, artist.” K. pointed to the door, behind which the girls were whispering, and said: “You seem very popular in the house.” “Oh, those brats!” the painter said, trying in vain to button his nightshirt at the neck. Apart from that he was barefoot and wore only a pair of loose, yellowish linen trousers secured with a belt, whose long end swung freely to and fro. “Those brats are a real burden to me,” he continued, giving up on the nightshirt, whose last button had just torn off, fetching a chair and insisting that K. sit down. “I once painted one of them—she isn't even here today—and ever since then they all pursue me. When I'm here myself they come in only when I let them, but whenever I'm away there's always at least one here. They've had a key made to my door and lend it to one another. You can hardly imagine how tiresome it is. For example, I come home with a lady whose portrait I'm to paint, unlock the door with my key and find, say, the hunchback there at the little table, painting her lips red with a brush, while her little brothers and sisters, whom she's supposed to be looking after, roam about and foul every corner of the room. Or I come home late in the evening, as happened only yesterday—please excuse my state and the disorder in the room on that account—well, I come home late in the evening and am about to get into bed when something pinches my leg; I look under the bed and pull out another of these creatures. Why they crowd round me like this I don't know; you will just have noticed, I think, that I make no effort to lure them here. Naturally it interferes with my work too. If this studio hadn't been put at my disposal free of charge, I'd have moved out long ago.” Just then a little voice called behind the door, delicate and anxious: “Titorelli, may we come in now?” “No,” the painter answered. “Not even just me?” it asked again. “Not even you,” the painter said, went to the door and locked it.

Meanwhile K. had looked round the room; it would never have occurred to him on his own that one could call this wretched little room a studio. One could scarcely take more than two long steps here either lengthways or across. Everything, floor, walls and ceiling, was made of wood; narrow gaps could be seen between the timbers. Opposite K., against the wall, stood the bed, piled high with bedclothes of different colours. In the middle of the room a picture stood on an easel, covered by a shirt whose sleeves dangled down to the floor. Behind K. was the window, through which, in the fog, one could see no further than the snow-covered roof of the neighbouring house.

The turning of the key in the lock reminded K. that he had meant to leave soon. He therefore took the manufacturer's letter from his pocket, handed it to the painter and said: “I heard about you through this gentleman, an acquaintance of yours, and have come on his advice.” The painter read the letter quickly and threw it on the bed. If the manufacturer had not spoken most definitely of Titorelli as an acquaintance, a poor man dependent on his alms, one could really have believed now that Titorelli did not know the manufacturer, or at least could not remember him. Moreover, the painter now asked: “Do you want to buy pictures, or have yourself painted?” K. looked at the painter in astonishment. What was actually in the letter? K. had taken it for granted that in the letter the manufacturer had told the painter that K. wanted nothing other than to enquire here about his proceedings. He had really rushed here far too hastily and thoughtlessly! But now he had to give the painter some sort of answer, and, glancing at the easel, he said: “You're working on a picture at present?” “Yes,” said the painter, throwing the shirt that hung over the easel after the letter on to the bed. “It's a portrait. A good piece of work, but not quite finished yet.” Chance favoured K.; the opportunity to speak of the court was positively being offered to him, for it was evidently the portrait of a judge. It was, incidentally, strikingly similar to the picture in the lawyer's study. This was admittedly an entirely different judge, a fat man with a full, black, bushy beard extending far up the sides of his cheeks; that picture, too, had been an oil painting, while this one had been lightly and indistinctly begun in pastels. But everything else was similar, for here too the judge was just about to rise threateningly from his throne, gripping its arms. “That's a judge,” K. had meant to say at once, but then held back for the moment and approached the picture as though he wished to study its details. He could not account for a large figure standing in the middle above the back of the throne, and asked the painter about it. It still needed a little working on, the painter replied, fetched a pastel from a small table and made a few strokes along the edges of the figure, without thereby making it any clearer to K. “It's Justice,” the painter said at last. “Now I recognise her,” K. said, “here is the blindfold over her eyes and here the scales. But aren't there wings on her heels, and isn't she running?” “Yes,” said the painter, “I was commissioned to paint it like that; it's actually Justice and the goddess of Victory in one.” “That isn't a good combination,” K. said with a smile, “Justice must be at rest, otherwise the scales sway and no just judgement is possible.” “I follow my client's wishes in this,” the painter said. “Yes, of course,” said K., who had not wanted to offend anyone with his remark. “You've painted the figure as it actually stands on the throne.” “No,” said the painter, “I've seen neither the figure nor the throne; it's all invented, but I was told what I must paint.” “What?” K. asked, deliberately behaving as though he did not quite understand the painter, “but it's a judge sitting in the judge's chair.” “Yes,” said the painter, “but he isn't a high-ranking judge and has never sat on a throne like that.” “And yet he has himself painted in such a solemn pose? He's sitting there like the president of a court.” “Yes, the gentlemen are vain,” said the painter. “But they have permission from above to have themselves painted like this. Exactly how each may have himself painted is prescribed. Unfortunately, though, you can't judge the details of the costume and the seat from this particular picture; pastels aren't suited to representations of this kind.” “Yes,” K. said, “it's strange that it's painted in pastels.” “The judge wanted it that way,” said the painter, “it's intended for a lady.” The sight of the picture seemed to have given him an appetite for work; he rolled up his shirtsleeves, took several pastels in his hand, and K. watched as, beneath their trembling tips, a reddish shadow formed around the judge's head, fading in rays towards the edge of the picture. Gradually this play of shadow surrounded the head like an adornment or a high distinction. Around the figure of Justice, however, it remained light apart from an imperceptible tint; in this light the figure seemed to stand out particularly strongly, it scarcely recalled the goddess of Justice any longer, but neither did it recall Victory, it now looked altogether like the goddess of the Hunt instead. The painter's work held K.'s attention more than he wanted; finally, however, he reproached himself for having been here so long already and having in essence done nothing yet for his own affair. “What is this judge called?” he asked suddenly. “I'm not allowed to say,” the painter replied; he was bent low over the picture and was plainly neglecting his guest, whom he had at first received so considerately. K. took this for a whim and was annoyed by it, because it was costing him time. “I suppose you're a man in the court's confidence?” he asked. The painter at once laid the pastels aside, straightened up, rubbed his hands together and looked at K. with a smile. “Best come straight out with the truth,” he said, “you want to learn something about the court, as indeed your letter of introduction says, and you started by talking about my pictures to win me over. But I don't take it amiss; you couldn't know that it was out of place with me. Oh, please!” he said, sharply warding K. off when he tried to object. And then he went on: “In any case you're quite right in your remark; I am a man in the court's confidence.” He paused, as though to give K. time to come to terms with this fact. The girls could now be heard again behind the door. They were probably crowding round the keyhole; perhaps one could also see into the room through the gaps. K. refrained from making any apology, since he did not want to distract the painter, but he also did not want the painter to become too conceited and in this way make himself, as it were, inaccessible, so he asked: “Is that a publicly recognised position?” “No,” said the painter shortly, as though this had deprived him of further speech. But K. did not want to let him fall silent, and said: “Well, unofficial positions of that kind are often more influential than recognised ones.” “That is precisely the case with me,” the painter said, nodding with a furrowed brow. “I spoke with the manufacturer about your case yesterday; he asked me whether I would help you, and I answered: ‘The man can come and see me some time,’ and now I'm pleased to see you here so soon. The matter seems to be weighing heavily on you, which of course doesn't surprise me at all. Perhaps you'd like to take off your coat first?” Although K. intended to remain here only a very short time, this invitation from the painter was very welcome. The air in the room had gradually become oppressive to him; several times he had already looked in surprise at a small iron stove in the corner, unquestionably unlit, and the stifling heat in the room was inexplicable. As he took off his winter coat and also unbuttoned his jacket, the painter said apologetically: “I have to have warmth. It's very cosy here, isn't it? The room is very well situated in that respect.” K. said nothing to this, but it was not really the warmth that made him uncomfortable; rather it was the stuffy air, which almost prevented him from breathing; the room had probably not been aired for a long time. This discomfort was made worse for K. by the painter's asking him to sit on the bed, while he himself sat down on the room's only chair in front of the easel. Besides, the painter seemed to misunderstand why K. remained only on the edge of the bed; he asked K. to make himself comfortable, and, when K. hesitated, went over himself and pressed him deep into the bedding and pillows. Then he returned to his chair and at last asked the first question that addressed the matter, which made K. forget everything else. “Are you innocent?” he asked. “Yes,” K. said. Answering this question positively delighted him, especially since he was answering a private individual, and therefore without any responsibility. No one had yet asked him so openly. To savour this delight he added: “I am completely innocent.” “I see,” said the painter, lowering his head and apparently reflecting. Suddenly he raised his head again and said: “If you're innocent, then the matter is very simple.” K.'s gaze clouded; this supposed confidant of the court spoke like an ignorant child. “My innocence doesn't simplify the matter,” K. said. Despite everything he had to smile, and slowly shook his head. “It depends on many subtleties in which the court loses itself. But in the end, from somewhere where there was originally nothing at all, it pulls out a great burden of guilt.” “Yes, yes, certainly,” the painter said, as though K. were needlessly disturbing his train of thought. “But you are innocent?” “Well, yes,” K. said. “That's the main thing,” said the painter. He was not to be influenced by counterarguments, but despite his decisiveness it was unclear whether he spoke like this from conviction or merely from indifference. K. wanted to establish that first, and therefore said: “You certainly know the court much better than I do; I know little more than what I've heard about it, admittedly from quite different people. But they all agreed that charges aren't brought lightly, and that once the court brings a charge it is firmly convinced of the accused's guilt and can only with difficulty be dissuaded from that conviction.” “With difficulty?” asked the painter, throwing one hand into the air. “The court can never be dissuaded from it. If I paint all the judges here side by side on a canvas, and you defend yourself before that canvas, you'll have more success than before the real court.” “Yes,” K. said to himself, forgetting that he had only meant to sound the painter out.

Again a girl behind the door began asking: “Titorelli, isn't he going to leave soon?” “Be quiet,” the painter called towards the door, “can't you see I'm having a discussion with the gentleman?” But the girl was not satisfied with that and asked: “Are you going to paint him?” And when the painter did not answer she added: “Please don't paint him, such an ugly man.” A confusion of unintelligible, approving shouts followed. The painter sprang to the door, opened it a crack—the girls' clasped hands could be seen stretched out pleadingly—and said: “If you won't be quiet, I'll throw you all down the stairs. Sit here on the steps and keep still.” They probably did not obey at once, so that he had to command: “Down on the steps!” Only then was it quiet.

“Forgive me,” the painter said as he returned to K. K. had scarcely turned towards the door; he had left it entirely to the painter whether and how he wished to protect him. Even now he scarcely moved when the painter bent down to him and, so as not to be heard outside, whispered in his ear: “These girls belong to the court too.” “What?” K. asked, drawing his head aside and looking at the painter. But the painter sat down on his chair again and said, half jokingly, half in explanation: “Everything belongs to the court.” “I hadn't noticed that yet,” K. said shortly; the painter's general remark took all the disquiet out of his reference to the girls. Nevertheless K. looked for a little while towards the door, behind which the girls now sat silently on the steps. Only one had pushed a straw through a gap between the timbers and was moving it slowly up and down.

“You don't seem to have an overall view of the court yet,” said the painter; he had stretched his legs wide apart and was slapping the floor with his toes. “But since you're innocent, you won't need one either. I'll get you out myself.” “How do you intend to do that?” K. asked. “When only a short while ago you yourself said that the court is completely inaccessible to reasoned evidence.” “Inaccessible only to evidence presented before the court,” said the painter, raising his forefinger as though K. had failed to notice a fine distinction. “It's a different matter, though, with what one attempts in this respect behind the public court, in the consultation rooms, in the corridors, or here in the studio, for example.” What the painter was now saying no longer seemed so unbelievable to K.; on the contrary, it showed great agreement with what K. had heard from other people too. Indeed, it was even very hopeful. If the judge was really so easily guided through personal connections as the lawyer had described, then the painter's connections with the vain judges were particularly important, and certainly by no means to be underestimated. In that case the painter fitted very well into the circle of helpers K. was gradually gathering round him. His talent for organisation had once been praised at the bank; here, where he was left entirely to himself, a good opportunity presented itself to put it to the utmost test. The painter observed the effect his explanation had had on K., and then said with a certain anxiety: “Don't you notice that I speak almost like a legal scholar? It's the uninterrupted contact with the gentlemen of the court that influences me so. Naturally I gain a great deal from it, but much of my artistic impetus is lost.” “How did you first come into contact with the judges?” K. asked; he wanted to gain the painter's confidence first before taking him directly into his service. “That was very simple,” said the painter, “I inherited the connection. My father was already a court painter. It's a position that is always handed down. New people can't be used for it. You see, so many different and varied rules, and above all secret ones, have been laid down for painting the various grades of officials that they never become known outside certain families. There in the drawer, for example, I have my father's notes, which I show no one. But only someone who knows them is qualified to paint judges. Yet even if I were to lose them, so many rules would remain that I carry only in my head that no one could challenge me for my position. Every judge wants to be painted as the great judges of old were painted, after all, and only I can do that.” “That's enviable,” said K., thinking of his position at the bank. “So your position is unshakeable?” “Yes, unshakeable,” the painter said, raising his shoulders proudly. “That's why I can also venture now and then to help a poor man who has a case against him.” “And how do you do that?” K. asked, as though it were not he whom the man had just called a poor man. But the painter would not be diverted, and said: “In your case, for example, since you're completely innocent, I shall do the following.” The repeated mention of his innocence was already becoming tiresome to K. It sometimes seemed to him as though, with such remarks, the painter was making a favourable outcome to the proceedings a precondition of his help, which naturally thereby collapsed into itself. Despite these doubts, however, K. controlled himself and did not interrupt the painter. He did not want to forgo the painter's help, of that he was determined, and this help did not seem to him at all more questionable than the lawyer's. K. even preferred it by far to the latter, because it was offered more harmlessly and openly.

The painter had drawn his chair closer to the bed, and continued in a lowered voice: “I forgot to ask you first what kind of release you want. There are three possibilities, namely actual acquittal, apparent acquittal and protraction. Actual acquittal is naturally the best, only I haven't the slightest influence on that kind of solution. In my opinion there isn't any individual at all who has influence over actual acquittal. Here probably only the innocence of the accused decides. Since you're innocent, it would really be possible for you to rely on your innocence alone. But then you need neither me nor any other help.”

This orderly account at first astonished K., but then he said as quietly as the painter: “I think you're contradicting yourself.” “How so?” the painter asked patiently, leaning back with a smile. This smile gave K. the feeling that he was now setting about discovering contradictions not in the painter's words but in the judicial proceedings themselves. Nevertheless he did not retreat, but said: “Earlier you remarked that the court is inaccessible to reasoned evidence; later you restricted this to the public court, and now you even say that an innocent man needs no help before the court. There's one contradiction already. But besides that, you said earlier that one can influence the judges personally, yet now you deny that actual acquittal, as you call it, can ever be achieved through personal influence. There's the second contradiction.” “These contradictions are easily explained,” said the painter. “We're talking about two different things here, what is written in the law and what I have personally experienced; you mustn't confuse them. In the law, which admittedly I haven't read, it naturally says on the one hand that the innocent man is acquitted, but on the other hand it doesn't say that the judges can be influenced. Now, however, I have experienced precisely the opposite. I know of no actual acquittal, but of many instances of influence. It is of course possible that in all the cases I know there was no innocence. But isn't that unlikely? In so many cases, not a single instance of innocence? Even as a child I listened closely to my father when he spoke of cases at home; the judges who came to his studio also spoke of the court, in our circles one speaks of nothing else at all; as soon as I had the opportunity to go to court myself, I always made use of it, I have listened to countless cases at important stages and followed them as far as they are visible, and—I must admit it—never witnessed a single actual acquittal.” “Not a single acquittal, then,” K. said, as though addressing himself and his hopes. “But that confirms the opinion I already have of the court. So it's futile from this side as well. A single executioner could replace the whole court.” “You mustn't generalise,” the painter said, dissatisfied, “I've only spoken of my own experiences.” “That's enough, surely,” K. said, “or have you heard of acquittals from earlier times?” “Such acquittals,” the painter answered, “are indeed supposed to have occurred. Only it's very hard to establish that. The court's final decisions aren't published, they aren't even accessible to the judges, and consequently only legends about old cases have survived. Admittedly most of these even contain actual acquittals; one can believe them, but they can't be proved. Nevertheless one needn't neglect them altogether; they certainly contain some truth, and they are very beautiful too, I've painted a few pictures myself with such legends as their subject.” “Mere legends don't change my opinion,” K. said, “and I suppose one can't appeal to these legends before the court either?” The painter laughed. “No, you can't do that,” he said. “Then it's useless to talk about them,” K. said; for the present he wanted to accept all the painter's opinions, even if he considered them improbable and they contradicted other reports. He had no time now to examine everything the painter said for its truth, still less to refute it; the utmost would already have been achieved if he persuaded the painter to help him in some way, even if not in a decisive one. He therefore said: “Let us leave actual acquittal aside, then, but you mentioned two other possibilities.” “Apparent acquittal and protraction. Those alone are in question,” said the painter. “But before we talk about them, wouldn't you like to take off your jacket? You must be hot.” “Yes,” said K., who until now had paid attention to nothing but the painter's explanations, but now, reminded of the heat, broke into a heavy sweat on his forehead. “It's almost unbearable.” The painter nodded as though he understood K.'s discomfort very well. “Couldn't we open the window?” K. asked. “No,” said the painter. “It's only a fixed pane of glass; it can't be opened.” Now K. realised that all this time he had been hoping that suddenly the painter or he himself would go to the window and fling it open. He was prepared to breathe in even the fog with his mouth open. The feeling of being completely shut off from the air here made him dizzy. He struck the featherbed beside him lightly with his hand and said in a weak voice: “That's inconvenient and unhealthy.” “Oh no,” the painter said in defence of his window. “Because it can't be opened, the warmth is kept in better here than by a double window, even though it's only a single pane. But if I want to air the room, which isn't very necessary since air comes in everywhere through the gaps between the timbers, I can open one of my doors, or even both.” Somewhat comforted by this explanation, K. looked round to find the second door. The painter noticed and said: “It's behind you; I had to block it with the bed.” Only now did K. see the small door in the wall. “Everything here is simply much too small for a studio,” the painter said, as though he wished to anticipate a criticism from K. “I had to arrange things as best I could. Naturally the bed in front of the door is in a very bad place. The judge I'm painting now, for example, always comes through the door by the bed, and I've given him a key to that door too, so that even when I'm not at home he can wait for me here in the studio. But he usually comes early in the morning, while I'm still asleep. Naturally it always tears me from the deepest sleep when the door beside the bed opens. You would lose all reverence for judges if you heard the curses with which I greet him when he climbs over my bed early in the morning. Admittedly I could take the key away from him, but that would only make things worse. Every door here can be broken off its hinges with the slightest effort.” Throughout this speech K. was considering whether he should take off his jacket, but finally he realised that unless he did he would be incapable of staying here any longer, so he took it off, but laid it across his knees so as to be able to put it on again if the discussion came to an end. Scarcely had he taken off his jacket when one of the girls called: “He's taken his jacket off already,” and they could all be heard crowding to the gaps to see the spectacle for themselves. “You see, the girls think,” the painter said, “that I'm going to paint you and that's why you're undressing.” “I see,” K. said, only slightly amused, for although he now sat in his shirtsleeves he felt little better than before. Almost peevishly he asked: “What did you call the other two possibilities?” He had already forgotten the expressions again. “Apparent acquittal and protraction,” the painter said. “It's up to you which you choose. Both can be achieved with my help, naturally not without effort; the difference in this respect is that apparent acquittal requires concentrated effort for a time, protraction much less effort but continuous effort. First, then, apparent acquittal. If that is what you wish, I write a statement confirming your innocence on a sheet of paper. The wording for such a statement has been handed down to me by my father and is quite unassailable. With this statement I now make the rounds of the judges I know. So I might begin by showing the statement to the judge I'm painting now, this evening when he comes for his sitting. I show him the statement, explain to him that you're innocent, and vouch for your innocence. But this isn't merely a formal guarantee; it's a real and binding one.” There was something like a reproach in the painter's eyes that K. should wish to impose the burden of such a guarantee upon him. “That would be very kind,” K. said. “And the judge would believe you, yet still not actually acquit me?” “As I said,” the painter replied. “Incidentally, it isn't at all certain that everyone would believe me; some judge, for example, will demand that I bring you to him in person. Then you would have to come along some time. Admittedly in such a case the matter is already half won, particularly since I would of course first tell you exactly how to behave with the judge concerned. It's worse with the judges who reject me from the outset—that will happen too. We must give up on these, although I certainly won't fail to make repeated attempts; but we can afford to do so, since individual judges cannot turn the balance here. Once I have enough judges' signatures on this statement, I take it to the judge who is currently conducting your case. Possibly I have his signature too, and then everything proceeds a little more quickly than otherwise. But in general there aren't many obstacles left at that point; it is then the time of greatest confidence for the accused. It is strange but true: people are more confident at this time than after the acquittal. No particular effort is needed now. In the statement the judge possesses the guarantee of a number of judges, can acquit you without concern and, after completing various formalities, will undoubtedly do so as a favour to me and other acquaintances. But you walk out of the court and are free.” “Then I'm free,” K. said hesitantly. “Yes,” said the painter, “but only apparently free, or, better put, temporarily free. The lowest-ranking judges, who include my acquaintances, don't have the right to grant a final acquittal; only the highest court has that right, a court completely beyond reach for you, for me and for all of us. We don't know what it's like there, and, incidentally, we don't want to know either. So our judges don't possess the great right to free someone from the charge, but they do possess the right to detach him from it. That means that if you're acquitted in this way, you're withdrawn from the charge for the moment, but it continues to hang over you and can take effect again at once as soon as the order comes from above. Since I'm on such good terms with the court, I can also tell you how, purely outwardly, the difference between actual and apparent acquittal appears in the regulations for the court offices. In an actual acquittal the case files are supposed to be put away entirely; they disappear completely from the proceedings, not only the charge but the proceedings and even the acquittal are destroyed, everything is destroyed. It's different with an apparent acquittal. No further change has been made to the file beyond its having been enriched by the statement of innocence, the acquittal and the reasons for the acquittal. Otherwise, however, it remains in the proceedings; it is passed on to the higher courts, as the constant traffic between the court offices requires, comes back to the lower ones and thus swings up and down with greater and smaller oscillations, with greater and smaller interruptions. These movements are incalculable. Seen from outside, it may sometimes look as though everything has long been forgotten, the file lost and the acquittal complete. Someone on the inside won't believe that. No file is lost, there is no forgetting at the court. One day—no one expects it—some judge takes the file attentively in hand, recognises that in this case the charge is still alive, and orders immediate arrest. Here I've assumed that a long time passes between the apparent acquittal and the fresh arrest; that is possible, and I know of such cases, but it's equally possible that the acquitted man comes home from the court and agents are already waiting there to arrest him again. Then, of course, the life of freedom is over.” “And the proceedings begin again?” K. asked, almost incredulously. “Certainly,” said the painter, “the proceedings begin again, but once again there is the possibility of obtaining an apparent acquittal, just as before. One must muster all one's strength again and not give in.” Perhaps the painter said the last words under the impression made upon him by K., who had slumped a little. “But,” K. asked, as though now wishing to forestall some revelation from the painter, “isn't obtaining a second acquittal harder than obtaining the first?” “One can't,” the painter answered, “say anything definite in that respect. You probably mean that the second arrest influences the judges' judgement against the accused? That isn't the case. The judges already foresaw this arrest when they acquitted him. So that circumstance has scarcely any effect. But for countless other reasons the judges' mood, as well as their legal assessment of the case, may have changed, and the efforts to secure the second acquittal must therefore be adapted to the changed circumstances and generally be just as vigorous as those before the first acquittal.” “But this second acquittal still isn't final either,” K. said, turning his head away in rejection. “Of course not,” said the painter, “the second acquittal is followed by the third arrest, the third acquittal by the fourth arrest, and so on. That's already inherent in the concept of apparent acquittal.” K. was silent. “Apparent acquittal evidently doesn't seem advantageous to you,” the painter said, “perhaps protraction suits you better. Shall I explain the nature of protraction?” K. nodded. The painter had settled broadly back into his chair, his nightshirt was wide open, and he had slipped one hand beneath it, stroking his chest and sides. “Protraction,” the painter said, looking straight ahead for a moment as though seeking an entirely accurate explanation, “protraction consists in keeping the proceedings permanently at their lowest stage. To achieve this it is necessary for the accused and his helper, but especially the helper, to remain in uninterrupted personal contact with the court. I repeat, this doesn't require the same expenditure of strength as obtaining an apparent acquittal, but it does require much greater attentiveness. One mustn't lose sight of the case, one must visit the judge concerned at regular intervals and also on special occasions, and seek in every way to keep him favourably disposed; if one isn't personally acquainted with the judge, one must have judges one does know influence him, without thereby being allowed to give up direct discussions. If one neglects nothing in this respect, one can assume with sufficient certainty that the proceedings won't get beyond their first stage. The proceedings admittedly don't cease, but the accused is almost as secure against conviction as if he were free. Compared with apparent acquittal, protraction has the advantage that the accused's future is less uncertain; he is spared the terror of sudden arrests, and needn't fear having to take upon himself the efforts and agitation associated with obtaining apparent acquittal, perhaps precisely at times when his other circumstances are least favourable to it. Admittedly protraction too has certain disadvantages for the accused which mustn't be underestimated. I'm not thinking here of the fact that the accused is never free in this case; he isn't really free in apparent acquittal either. It's another disadvantage. The proceedings can't stand still without at least apparent reasons for it. Something must therefore happen in the proceedings outwardly. Thus various orders must be made from time to time, the accused must be questioned, investigations must take place and so forth. The proceedings must simply be turned continually round within the small circle to which they have been artificially confined. Naturally this entails certain inconveniences for the accused, which, however, you mustn't imagine as too serious either. It's all merely outward, after all, so the interrogations, for example, are only very short; if on one occasion one has no time or no desire to go, one can excuse oneself, and with certain judges one can even agree together on the arrangements for a long time in advance; essentially it's only a matter of reporting to one's judge from time to time, since one is an accused person.” During the last words K. had already laid his jacket over his arm and stood up. “He's getting up already,” came the immediate cry from outside the door. “You want to leave already?” asked the painter, who had stood up too. “It's certainly the air that's driving you away. It's very embarrassing for me. I still had quite a few things to tell you. I've had to be very brief. But I hope I've made myself understood.” “Oh yes,” said K., whose head ached from the effort with which he had forced himself to listen. Despite this assurance, the painter summed everything up once more, as though he wanted to give K. some comfort to take home with him: “What the two methods have in common is that they prevent the accused from being convicted.” “But they also prevent actual acquittal,” K. said softly, as though ashamed of having realised it. “You've grasped the essence of the matter,” the painter said quickly. K. laid his hand on his winter coat, but could not even bring himself to put on his jacket. He would have liked best to bundle everything up and run with it into the fresh air. Even the girls could not move him to get dressed, although, prematurely, they were already calling to one another that he was putting his clothes on. The painter was anxious to interpret K.'s mood somehow, and therefore said: “You probably haven't decided yet about my proposals. I approve of that. I would even have advised you against deciding immediately. The advantages and disadvantages are very subtle. Everything must be weighed up carefully. Admittedly one mustn't lose too much time either.” “I'll come back soon,” K. said, suddenly deciding to put on his jacket, throwing his coat over his shoulder and hurrying to the door, behind which the girls now began to shriek. K. thought he could see the shrieking girls through the door. “But you must keep your word,” said the painter, who had not followed him, “otherwise I'll come to the bank to enquire for myself.” “Do unlock the door,” K. said, tugging at the handle, which, as he could tell from the counterpressure, the girls were holding fast outside. “Do you want to be bothered by the girls?” the painter asked. “You'd better use this exit,” and he pointed to the door behind the bed. K. agreed and sprang back to the bed. But instead of opening the door there, the painter crawled under the bed and asked from below: “Just one more moment. Wouldn't you like to see a picture I could sell you?” K. did not want to be rude; the painter really had taken an interest in him and promised to help him further, and because of K.'s forgetfulness they had not yet spoken at all about payment for the help, so K. could not refuse him now and allowed him to show the picture, although he was trembling with impatience to get out of the studio. The painter pulled a heap of unframed pictures from under the bed, so covered in dust that when he tried to blow it off the top picture it swirled before K.'s eyes for a long time, robbing him of breath. “A heath landscape,” the painter said, handing K. the picture. It showed two frail trees standing far apart in dark grass. In the background was a many-coloured sunset. “Beautiful,” K. said, “I'll buy it.” K. had thoughtlessly spoken so briefly, and was therefore glad when the painter, instead of taking offence, picked up a second picture from the floor. “Here is a companion piece to that picture,” the painter said. It might have been intended as a companion piece, but not the slightest difference from the first picture could be discerned; here were the trees, here the grass and there the sunset. But K. cared little about that. “They're beautiful landscapes,” he said, “I'll buy both and hang them in my office.” “The subject seems to please you,” the painter said, bringing up a third picture, “it's fortunate I have another similar picture here.” But it was not similar; rather, it was the very same old heath landscape. The painter was making good use of this opportunity to sell old pictures. “I'll take this one too,” K. said. “How much are the three pictures?” “We'll discuss that next time,” the painter said. “You're in a hurry now, and we're going to remain in touch. Besides, I'm pleased you like the pictures; I'll give you all the pictures I have down here to take with you. They're all heath landscapes, I've painted a great many heath landscapes. Some people reject pictures like these because they're too gloomy, but others, and you are one of them, love precisely that gloom.” But K. had no interest now in the professional experiences of the beggar-painter. “Pack up all the pictures,” he cried, interrupting the painter, “my attendant will come tomorrow and collect them.” “That isn't necessary,” said the painter. “I hope I can find you a porter who'll go with you straight away.” And at last he leaned over the bed and unlocked the door. “Don't hesitate to step on the bed,” the painter said, “everyone who comes in here does.” K. would have shown no consideration even without this invitation; he had actually already set one foot in the middle of the featherbed when he looked out through the open door and drew his foot back again. “What is that?” he asked the painter. “What are you surprised at?” the painter asked, surprised in his turn. “These are the court offices. Didn't you know there were court offices here? There are court offices in almost every attic, so why should they be missing here of all places? My studio actually belongs to the court offices too, but the court has put it at my disposal.” K. was not so much alarmed at having found court offices here too; he was alarmed chiefly at himself, at his ignorance of court affairs. It seemed to him a basic rule for the behaviour of an accused man always to be prepared, never to let himself be surprised, not to look unsuspectingly to the right when the judge stood beside him on the left—and it was precisely this basic rule that he kept breaking. Before him stretched a long corridor, the air blowing from it making the studio's air seem refreshing by comparison. Benches had been placed on both sides of the corridor, exactly as in the waiting room of the office responsible for K. There seemed to be precise regulations for furnishing the offices. At present there were not many parties coming and going here. A man sat there half reclining, his face buried in his arms on the bench, and seemed to be asleep; another stood in the half-darkness at the end of the corridor. K. now climbed over the bed, and the painter followed him with the pictures. They soon met a court attendant—K. now recognised all court attendants by the gold button they wore among the ordinary buttons on their civilian clothes—and the painter instructed him to accompany K. with the pictures. K. staggered rather than walked, holding his handkerchief pressed to his mouth. They were already near the exit when the girls came storming towards them, so that K. had not been spared them after all. They had evidently seen that the studio's second door had been opened and had gone round to enter from this side. “I can't come any further with you,” the painter called, laughing under the onslaught of the girls. “Goodbye. And don't think it over too long!” K. did not even look back at him. In the street he took the first carriage that came his way. He was anxious to get rid of the attendant, whose gold button continually caught his eye, although it probably attracted no one else's attention. In his eagerness to serve, the attendant even wanted to sit on the coachman's box, but K. chased him off. It was long past midday when K. arrived outside the bank. He would have liked to leave the pictures in the carriage, but feared that on some occasion he might be obliged to produce them before the painter. He therefore had them brought to his office and locked them in the lowest drawer of his desk, to put them beyond the deputy manager's sight at least for the next few days.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: At last K. had decided to withdraw his case from the lawyer. His doubts about whether he was right to do so could not be eradicated, it was true, but his conviction that it was necessary prevailed. On the day he intended to go to the lawyer, the decision had drained much of K.'s capacity for work; he worked particularly slowly, had to stay at the office a very long time, and it was already past ten o'clock when he finally stood outside the lawyer's door. Even before ringing he considered whether it might not be better to dismiss the lawyer by telephone or by letter; the conversation in person was bound to be very awkward. Nevertheless, in the end K. did not want to forgo it: any other form of dismissal would be accepted in silence or with a few formal words, and, unless Leni could perhaps find something out, K. would never learn how the lawyer had received his dismissal, or what consequences that dismissal might have for K. in the lawyer's not unimportant opinion. But if the lawyer were sitting opposite K. and taken by surprise by the dismissal, then, even if little could be drawn out of him, K. would easily be able to gather everything he wanted from his face and behaviour. It was not even out of the question that he might be persuaded that it would, after all, be better to leave the defence to the lawyer, and might then withdraw his dismissal.

The first ring at the lawyer's door was fruitless, as usual. “Leni could be quicker,” K. thought. But it was already an advantage if the people in the other flat did not interfere, as they usually did, whether it was the man in the dressing gown or someone else who began making a nuisance of himself. As K. pressed the button a second time, he looked back at the other door, but this time it too remained closed. At last two eyes appeared at the little viewing window in the lawyer's door, but they were not Leni's eyes. Someone unlocked the door, but for the moment still braced himself against it, called back into the flat, “It's him,” and only then opened it fully. K. had been pressing against the door, for already he could hear a key being hastily turned in the lock of the other flat behind him. So when the door in front of him finally opened, he positively stormed into the hall, and just caught sight of Leni, to whom the warning call from the person opening the door had been directed, running away in her shift down the passage between the rooms. He watched her for a little while, then turned to look at the person who had opened the door. He was a small, thin man with a full beard, holding a candle in his hand. “Are you employed here?” K. asked. “No,” the man answered, “I don't belong here, the lawyer merely represents me, I'm here on a legal matter.” “Without a jacket?” K. asked, indicating the man's incomplete dress with a movement of his hand. “Oh, forgive me,” the man said, shining the candle on himself as though he too were seeing his condition for the first time. “Is Leni your mistress?” K. asked curtly. He had planted his feet a little apart, his hands clasped behind his back, holding his hat. The mere possession of a substantial overcoat made him feel greatly superior to the scrawny little man. “Oh God,” the man said, raising one hand before his face in frightened denial, “no, no, whatever are you thinking?” “You look believable,” K. said, smiling, “all the same—come along.” He beckoned to him with his hat and made him go ahead. “What is your name, then?” K. asked on the way. “Block, Block the merchant,” the little man said, turning towards K. as he introduced himself, but K. would not let him stop. “Is that your real name?” K. asked. “Certainly,” came the answer, “why do you doubt it?” “I thought you might have a reason for keeping your name to yourself,” K. said. He felt as free as one otherwise feels only when talking to lowly people in a foreign place, keeping everything concerning oneself to oneself, speaking with indifference only of the other people's interests, thereby raising them in their own estimation, but also able to drop them at will. K. stopped at the door of the lawyer's study, opened it and called to the merchant, who had obediently gone on: “Not so fast, bring the light in here.” K. thought Leni might have hidden here, and had the merchant search every corner, but the room was empty. In front of the portrait of the judge K. held the merchant back by his braces. “Do you know him?” he asked, pointing upwards with his forefinger. The merchant raised the candle, peered up with narrowed eyes and said: “That is a judge.” “A senior judge?” K. asked, positioning himself in front of the merchant to one side, so that he could observe the impression the picture made on him. The merchant looked up admiringly. “It is a senior judge,” he said. “You don't know much about things,” K. said. “Of all the low-ranking examining magistrates, he is the lowest.” “Now I remember,” the merchant said, lowering the candle, “I have heard that before too.” “But of course,” K. cried, “I'd forgotten, of course you must have heard it before.” “But why, why?” the merchant asked, while moving towards the door, propelled by K.'s hands. Outside in the passage K. said: “You know where Leni has hidden, don't you?” “Hidden?” the merchant said, “no, but she is probably in the kitchen making the lawyer some soup.” “Why didn't you say so at once?” K. asked. “I was going to take you there, but you called me back,” the merchant answered, seemingly confused by the contradictory orders. “You must think you're very clever,” K. said, “take me there, then!” K. had never been in the kitchen before; it was surprisingly large and lavishly equipped. The stove alone was three times the size of ordinary stoves; none of the other details could be made out, for the kitchen was lit now only by a little lamp hanging beside the entrance. Leni stood at the stove in her usual white apron, emptying eggs into a pot over a spirit flame. “Good evening, Josef,” she said, glancing sideways. “Good evening,” K. said, indicating with one hand a chair standing apart, on which the merchant was to sit, which he did. But K. went right up behind Leni, bent over her shoulder and asked: “Who is that man?” Leni put one arm round K., while her other hand stirred the soup, drew him forwards towards her and said: “He's a pitiable creature, a poor merchant, a certain Block. Just look at him.” They both looked back. The merchant sat on the chair to which K. had directed him; he had blown out the candle, whose light was now unnecessary, and was squeezing the wick between his fingers to prevent it smoking. “You were in your shift,” K. said, turning her head back towards the stove with his hand. She said nothing. “Is he your lover?” K. asked. She tried to reach for the soup pot, but K. took both her hands and said: “Well, answer me!” She said: “Come into the study, I'll explain everything to you.” “No,” K. said, “I want you to explain it here.” She clung to him and tried to kiss him. But K. warded her off and said: “I don't want you to kiss me now.” “Josef,” Leni said, looking beseechingly and yet openly into K.'s eyes, “surely you're not jealous of Mr Block.” “Rudi,” she then said, turning to the merchant, “do help me, you can see I'm under suspicion, leave the candle alone.” One might have thought he had not been paying attention, but he was fully abreast of everything. “I wouldn't know why you should be jealous either,” he said, without much quickness of wit. “Actually, neither do I,” K. said, looking at the merchant with a smile. Leni laughed aloud, took advantage of K.'s inattention to slip her arm through his and whispered: “Leave him alone now, you can see what sort of person he is. I've taken him under my wing a little because he's an important client of the lawyer's, for no other reason. And you? Do you still want to speak to the lawyer tonight? He's very ill today, but if you want, I'll announce you all the same. But you're certainly staying the night with me. You haven't been to see us for so long either, even the lawyer has been asking about you. Don't neglect the trial! I have all sorts of things to tell you too, things I've found out. But now, first of all, take off your coat!” She helped him take it off, took his hat, ran with the things to the hall to hang them up, then ran back again and looked to the soup. “Shall I announce you first or take him his soup first?” “Announce me first,” K. said. He was annoyed; he had originally intended to discuss his affair thoroughly with Leni, in particular the dismissal he was considering, but the merchant's presence had taken away his inclination to do so. Now, however, he felt his affair was too important to allow this little merchant to have a possibly decisive influence on it, and he called Leni, who was already in the passage, back again. “Take him his soup first after all,” he said, “let him gather his strength for his conversation with me, he'll need it.” “You are also a client of the lawyer's,” the merchant said softly from his corner, as if establishing a fact. But this was not well received. “What business is that of yours?” K. said, and Leni said: “Will you be quiet.” “Then I'll take him his soup first,” Leni said to K., pouring the soup into a plate. “The only thing to fear then is that he'll soon fall asleep, he goes to sleep soon after eating.” “What I have to say to him will keep him awake,” K. said; he kept wanting to hint that he intended to discuss something important with the lawyer, he wanted Leni to ask what it was, and only then to ask her advice. But she punctually carried out only the orders that were spoken. As she passed him with the tray she deliberately brushed gently against him and whispered: “Once he's eaten his soup I'll announce you straight away, so I can have you back as soon as possible.” “Off you go,” K. said, “off you go.” “Do be nicer,” she said, turning all the way round once more in the doorway with the tray.

K. watched her go; now it was finally settled that the lawyer would be dismissed, and it was probably better, too, that he could no longer discuss it with Leni beforehand; she scarcely had a sufficient grasp of the whole, would certainly have advised him against it, might possibly even have succeeded in stopping K. dismissing him this time; he would have continued in doubt and uneasiness, and in the end, after a while, would have carried out his decision all the same, for the decision was too compelling. But the sooner it was carried out, the more harm would be averted. Perhaps, in any case, the merchant might have something to say about it.

K. turned round; scarcely had the merchant noticed this when he made to rise at once. “Stay seated,” K. said, drawing a chair up beside him. “Have you been the lawyer's client a long time?” K. asked. “Yes,” the merchant said, “a very long time.” “How many years has he been representing you, then?” K. asked. “I don't know what you mean,” the merchant said, “in business legal matters—I have a grain business—the lawyer has represented me ever since I took over the business, so about twenty years; in my own trial, which is probably what you are referring to, he has also represented me from the start, it's more than five years now. Yes, well over five years,” he then added, taking out an old wallet, “I have it all written down here; if you like I can give you the exact dates. It's hard to keep everything in one's head. My trial has probably been going on much longer, it began shortly after my wife's death, and that was more than five and a half years ago.” K. moved closer to him. “So the lawyer takes on ordinary legal cases too?” he asked. This connection between business and the law seemed immensely reassuring to K. “Certainly,” the merchant said, then whispered to K.: “They even say he is more capable in those legal cases than in the others.” But then he seemed to regret what he had said, laid a hand on K.'s shoulder and said: “I beg you, don't give me away.” K. patted his thigh to reassure him and said: “No, I'm no informer.” “You see, he's vindictive,” the merchant said. “He certainly won't do anything to such a faithful client,” K. said. “Oh yes he will,” the merchant said, “when he's worked up he makes no distinctions; besides, I'm not really faithful to him.” “How are you not?” K. asked. “Shall I confide in you?” the merchant asked doubtfully. “I think you may,” K. said. “Well,” the merchant said, “I'll confide part of it to you, but you must tell me a secret too, so that we each have a hold on the other where the lawyer is concerned.” “You're very cautious,” K. said, “but I'll tell you a secret that will put your mind entirely at rest. So what does your unfaithfulness to the lawyer consist of?” “I have,” the merchant said hesitantly, in the tone of someone confessing to something dishonourable, “I have other lawyers besides him.” “Surely that's not so bad,” K. said, a little disappointed. “Here it is,” the merchant said; he had still been breathing heavily since his confession, but K.'s remark gave him more confidence. “It isn't allowed. And least of all is one allowed to engage backstreet lawyers as well as a so-called lawyer. And that is precisely what I've done; besides him I have five backstreet lawyers.” “Five!” K. cried; it was only the number that astonished him, “five lawyers besides this one?” The merchant nodded: “I'm in negotiations with a sixth as well.” “But why do you need so many lawyers?” K. asked. “I need them all,” the merchant said. “Would you explain that to me?” K. asked. “Gladly,” the merchant said. “Above all, I don't want to lose my trial, that goes without saying. Consequently I must not neglect anything that might help me; even if in a particular instance the hope of benefit is very slight, I must not discard it. That is why I've spent everything I possess on the trial. For instance, I've taken all the money out of my business; the offices of my business used to fill almost an entire floor, now a little room in a back building is enough, where I work with an apprentice. Of course it was not only the withdrawal of the money that caused this decline, but still more the withdrawal of my capacity for work. If you want to do something for your trial, you can devote little attention to anything else.” “So you still work at the court yourself?” K. asked. “That is just what I'd like to learn something about.” “I can tell you very little about that,” the merchant said, “at first I did try it too, but I soon gave it up again. It is too exhausting and brings little success. Working and negotiating there oneself proved quite impossible, for me at least. Even just sitting and waiting there is a great strain. You know yourself how heavy the air is in the offices.” “How do you know I've been there?” K. asked. “I was in the waiting room when you passed through.” “What a coincidence!” K. cried, quite carried away and entirely forgetting how ridiculous the merchant had seemed before, “so you saw me! You were in the waiting room when I passed through. Yes, I did pass through there once.” “It's not such a great coincidence,” the merchant said, “I'm there almost every day.” “I'll probably have to go there more often now too,” K. said, “only I'm unlikely to be received with as much honour as I was that time. Everyone stood up. They probably thought I was a judge.” “No,” the merchant said, “we were greeting the court usher that time. We knew you were an accused man. News of that kind spreads very quickly.” “So you knew that already,” K. said, “but in that case my behaviour may have seemed arrogant to you. Wasn't it discussed?” “No,” the merchant said, “on the contrary. But those are foolish things.” “What foolish things?” K. asked. “Why do you ask?” the merchant said irritably. “You don't seem to know the people there yet, and you may take it the wrong way. You must remember that in these proceedings all sorts of things keep coming up that the mind can no longer cope with; one is simply too tired and distracted for many things, and to make up for it one turns to superstition. I'm speaking of the others, but I'm no better myself. One superstition of this sort, for instance, is that many people claim to be able to tell the outcome of the trial from the accused man's face, particularly from the outline of his lips. Now these people claimed that, judging by your lips, you would certainly be convicted, and soon. I repeat, it is a ridiculous superstition, and in most cases the facts completely disprove it, but when one lives among those people it is hard to escape such opinions. Just think how powerful that superstition can be. You spoke to someone there, didn't you? But he could scarcely answer you. Of course there are many reasons for being confused there, but one of them was the sight of your lips. He said later that he had thought he could see the sign of his own conviction on your lips too.” “My lips?” K. asked, taking out a pocket mirror and looking at himself. “I can't see anything special about my lips. Can you?” “Neither can I,” the merchant said, “nothing at all.” “How superstitious these people are!” K. exclaimed. “Didn't I say so?” the merchant asked. “Do they spend so much time together, then, exchanging opinions?” K. said. “So far I've kept entirely apart.” “In general they don't associate with one another,” the merchant said, “that wouldn't be possible, there are so many of them. There are few common interests either. If a belief in some common interest does occasionally arise in a group, it soon proves to be a mistake. Nothing can be achieved against the court by acting together. Every case is examined on its own, it is the most painstaking of courts. So nothing can be achieved together, only an individual sometimes achieves something in secret; the others don't hear of it until it has been achieved; nobody knows how it happened. So there is no community, though people do meet here and there in the waiting rooms, but little is discussed there. The superstitious opinions have existed since ancient times and positively multiply of their own accord.” “I saw the gentlemen there in the waiting room,” K. said, “their waiting seemed so useless to me.” “The waiting is not useless,” the merchant said, “only taking action on one's own is useless. I've already said that I now have five lawyers besides this one. You would think—at first I thought so myself—that I could now leave the matter entirely to them. But that would be quite wrong. I can leave it to them less than if I had only one. You don't understand that, do you?” “No,” K. said, laying his hand soothingly on the merchant's hand to check his over-hasty speech, “I would just like to ask you to speak a little more slowly, these are all things of great importance to me, and I can't quite follow them.” “It's good of you to remind me,” the merchant said, “you're a newcomer, a beginner. Your trial is six months old, isn't it? Yes, I've heard about it. Such a young trial! Whereas I've thought these things through countless times already, to me they are the most self-evident things in the world.” “You must be glad your trial has progressed so far?” K. asked; he did not want to ask outright how the merchant's affairs stood. But he received no clear answer either. “Yes, I've rolled my trial along for five years,” the merchant said, lowering his head, “that is no small achievement.” Then he was silent for a little while. K. listened to hear whether Leni was coming yet. On the one hand he did not want her to come, for he still had much to ask, and he did not want Leni to find him in this confidential conversation with the merchant either; on the other hand he was annoyed that, despite his presence, she was staying so long with the lawyer, far longer than was needed to serve the soup. “I still remember that time precisely,” the merchant began again, and K. was immediately all attention, “when my trial was about as old as your trial is now. At that time I had only this lawyer, but I was not very satisfied with him.” Here I'm finding out everything, K. thought, nodding his head vigorously, as though in this way he could encourage the merchant to say everything worth knowing. “My trial,” the merchant went on, “was not moving forward; investigations were indeed being held, and I attended every one, gathered material, lodged all my business ledgers with the court, which, as I later learnt, wasn't even necessary, I kept running to the lawyer, and he submitted various petitions too—” “Various petitions?” K. asked. “Yes, certainly,” the merchant said. “That is very important to me,” K. said, “in my case he is still working on the first petition. He's done nothing yet. I see now that he is neglecting me disgracefully.” “There may be various valid reasons why the petition is not yet finished,” the merchant said. “Besides, in the case of my petitions it later turned out that they were quite worthless. I even read one myself through the kindness of a court official. It was learned enough, but really devoid of content. First of all a great deal of Latin, which I don't understand, then general appeals to the court pages long, then flattery of certain particular officials, who were not named, though anyone in the know must certainly have been able to guess them, then self-praise on the lawyer's part, in which he abased himself before the court in a positively doglike way, and finally examinations of legal cases from long ago that were supposed to resemble mine. Those examinations were indeed very painstakingly done, as far as I could follow them. I don't mean by all this to pass judgement on the lawyer's work, and the petition I read was only one among several; in any case, though, and this is what I want to speak about now, at that time I could see no progress in my trial.” “What sort of progress did you want to see?” K. asked. “That is a very sensible question,” the merchant said, smiling, “one can rarely see any progress in these proceedings. But I didn't know that then.
